uni-common-maths-a.title: Engineering Mathematics I (B.Tech first year)
uni-common-maths-a.description: First-year engineering mathematics, unit by unit: calculus of one and several variables, multiple integrals, matrices and infinite series, with solved examples, quizzes and unit exams.

courses.title: Maths I · Unit 1 · Differential calculus of one variable
courses.summary: Successive differentiation, Leibniz theorem, mean value theorems, Taylor–Maclaurin expansions and indeterminate forms, covering topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech/B.E. first-year programmes.
outcomes: Find nth derivatives using standard results and Leibniz theorem
State and apply Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems
Expand functions in Taylor and Maclaurin series
Evaluate indeterminate forms with L'Hôpital's rule
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Riya models beam deflection as y = x²·e^(3x) and needs the 5th derivative for a series solution.
Differentiating five times by hand is messy — Leibniz theorem does it in one line.

steps.title: Standard nth derivatives
steps.body:
- dⁿ/dxⁿ (e^(ax)) = aⁿ e^(ax)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ (ax+b)^m = m(m−1)…(m−n+1) aⁿ (ax+b)^(m−n)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ 1/(ax+b) = (−1)ⁿ n! aⁿ /(ax+b)^(n+1)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ log(ax+b) = (−1)^(n−1) (n−1)! aⁿ /(ax+b)ⁿ
- dⁿ/dxⁿ sin(ax+b) = aⁿ sin(ax+b+nπ/2); same with cos.

For rational functions, first split into **partial fractions**, then apply the 1/(ax+b) rule to each term.

steps.title: Leibniz theorem
steps.body:
If u and v have nth derivatives, (uv)ₙ = Σ (r=0 to n) ⁿCᵣ u₍ₙ₋ᵣ₎ vᵣ = uₙv + ⁿC₁u₍ₙ₋₁₎v₁ + ⁿC₂u₍ₙ₋₂₎v₂ + … + uvₙ.

Choose **v** to be the polynomial factor, because its derivatives vanish after a few steps.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Find y₅ for y = x²e^(3x).
Take u = e^(3x), v = x². v₁ = 2x, v₂ = 2, v₃ = 0.
y₅ = 3⁵e^(3x)x² + 5·3⁴e^(3x)·2x + 10·3³e^(3x)·2 = e^(3x)(243x² + 810x + 540).

**Example 2.** Find yₙ for y = 1/(x²−1).
Partial fractions: y = ½[1/(x−1) − 1/(x+1)].
yₙ = ½(−1)ⁿ n! [1/(x−1)^(n+1) − 1/(x+1)^(n+1)].

steps.title: Classic exam result
steps.body:
**Example 3.** If y = sin⁻¹x, show (1−x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0 and hence (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ − (2n+1)x y₍ₙ₊₁₎ − n²yₙ = 0.
Step 1: y₁ = 1/√(1−x²) ⇒ (1−x²)y₁² = 1.
Step 2: differentiate: (1−x²)2y₁y₂ − 2xy₁² = 0 ⇒ (1−x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0.
Step 3: apply Leibniz n times to each product: (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ + n(−2x)y₍ₙ₊₁₎ + [n(n−1)/2](−2)yₙ − [x y₍ₙ₊₁₎ + n yₙ] = 0, which simplifies to the result.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor aⁿ from the chain rule.
- Using Leibniz with the exponential as v — the series never terminates.
- Missing the binomial coefficient ⁿC₂ = n(n−1)/2 when collecting terms.

activity.prompt: Match each function with its nth derivative

quiz.why: Each differentiation multiplies e^(−x) by −1, so the third derivative is (−1)³e^(−x) = −e^(−x).

quiz.q: In Leibniz theorem for (uv)ₙ the coefficient of u₍ₙ₋₂₎v₂ is
quiz.why: In (uv)ₙ, the term with u_{n−2}v₂ has coefficient ⁿC₂ = n(n − 1)/2.

quiz.q: For y = x³ sin x, which factor should be v in Leibniz?
quiz.why: Take v = x³, since its derivatives vanish after the third, leaving only four terms in Leibniz's formula.
d/dx cos 3x = 3cos(3x + π/2), so each derivative gives a factor 3 and a phase shift π/2: 3ⁿcos(3x + nπ/2).
For log(ax + b), the nth derivative is (−1)^(n−1)(n − 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ. With a = 2 this gives the stated result.

scenes.text: A car covers 120 km in 1.5 h on an expressway with an 80 km/h limit.
Without any camera seeing it speed, the mean value theorem proves that at some instant the speed was exactly 80 km/h.

steps.title: Rolle's theorem
steps.body:
If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c in (a,b) with f′(c) = 0.

Geometrically: a smooth curve that starts and ends at the same height has a horizontal tangent somewhere in between.

steps.title: Lagrange (LMVT) and Cauchy MVT
steps.body:
**LMVT:** f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) ⇒ ∃ c ∈ (a,b): f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). The tangent at c is parallel to the chord.

**Cauchy MVT:** f, g continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), g′(x) ≠ 0 ⇒ ∃ c: f′(c)/g′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/[g(b) − g(a)].

LMVT is Cauchy's with g(x) = x; Rolle's is LMVT with f(a) = f(b).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x² − 5x + 6 on [2,3].
f(2) = 0 = f(3); polynomial ⇒ continuous and differentiable. f′(c) = 2c − 5 = 0 ⇒ c = 2.5 ∈ (2,3). ✔

**Example 2.** Find c for LMVT with f(x) = x³ on [1,3].
[f(3) − f(1)]/(3 − 1) = (27 − 1)/2 = 13. f′(c) = 3c² = 13 ⇒ c = √(13/3) ≈ 2.08 ∈ (1,3). ✔

**Example 3.** Using LMVT show sin x < x for x > 0 (x ≤ π/2 suffices).
f(t) = t − sin t on [0,x]: f(x) − f(0) = x·f′(c) = x(1 − cos c) > 0 ⇒ x > sin x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Rolle's to f(x) = |x| on [−1,1]: it is not differentiable at 0, so the theorem does not apply.
- Reporting a c that lies outside the open interval.
- In Cauchy MVT, forgetting to check g′(x) ≠ 0 in (a,b).

activity.prompt: LMVT for f(x) = x² on [1, 5]: find c.

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem needs f(a) = f(b) and
quiz.why: Rolle's theorem needs f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b). Then f′(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
options: only differentiability at a and b

quiz.why: The Lagrange MVT says there is a point where the tangent is parallel to the chord joining the end points, because f′(c) equals the chord's slope.
options: a tangent parallel to the chord exists
the curve is a straight line

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem fails for |x| on [−1,1] because
quiz.why: |x| has a corner at 0, so it is not differentiable there, and Rolle's theorem needs differentiability on the open interval. (f(−1) = f(1) and it is continuous.)
options: it is not differentiable at x = 0

quiz.q: c for LMVT with f(x) = eˣ on [0,1]?
quiz.why: f′(c) = (e − 1)/(1 − 0) gives eᶜ = e − 1, so c = ln(e − 1) ≈ 0.541, which lies in (0, 1).

quiz.q: Cauchy MVT with g(x) = x reduces to
quiz.why: With g(x) = x, g′ = 1 and g(b) − g(a) = b − a, so Cauchy's formula becomes Lagrange's: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).

scenes.text: A microcontroller has no 'sin' button — it only adds and multiplies.
Engineers store a few Maclaurin terms of sin x and get 6-digit accuracy for small angles.

steps.title: Taylor's theorem
steps.body:
f(a + h) = f(a) + h f′(a) + h²/2! f″(a) + … + hⁿ⁻¹/(n−1)! f⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾(a) + Rₙ.

Lagrange remainder: Rₙ = hⁿ/n! f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh), 0 < θ < 1. Writing x = a + h gives the series in powers of (x − a). With a = 0 we get the **Maclaurin** series.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Expand log x in powers of (x − 1) up to 4 terms.
f(1) = 0, f′ = 1/x → 1, f″ = −1/x² → −1, f‴ = 2/x³ → 2, f⁗ = −6/x⁴ → −6.
log x = (x−1) − (x−1)²/2 + (x−1)³/3 − (x−1)⁴/4 + …

**Example 2.** Maclaurin series of eˣ sin x up to x³.
Multiply series: (1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6)(x − x³/6) = x + x² + (1/2 − 1/6)x³ + … = x + x² + x³/3 + …

**Example 3.** Estimate √(1.1) using (1+x)^(1/2): 1 + 0.05 − 0.00125 + 0.0000625 ≈ 1.04881 (true value 1.048809).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing hⁿ/n instead of hⁿ/n! in the coefficients.
- Using log(1 + x) outside −1 < x ≤ 1.
- Expanding about 0 when the question asks for powers of (x − a).

activity.text: cos x = 1 − x²/___ + x⁴/24 − …   and   eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/___ + …

quiz.q: Coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin series of sin x?
quiz.why: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, so the coefficient of x³ is −1/6.

quiz.q: Maclaurin series is Taylor series about
quiz.why: The Maclaurin series is the Taylor series expanded about the point x = 0.

quiz.q: tan x up to x³ is
quiz.why: tan x = x + x³/3 + 2x⁵/15 + …, so up to x³ it is x + x³/3.
The Lagrange form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem is Rₙ = (hⁿ/n!) f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh) with 0 < θ < 1.

quiz.q: First two non-zero terms of e^x·cos x?
quiz.why: Multiplying (1 + x + x²/2 + …)(1 − x²/2 + …) gives 1 + x + 0·x² − x³/3 + …, so the first two non-zero terms are 1 + x.

scenes.text: Arjun is told sin x / x → 1 as x → 0 but wonders why we cannot just put x = 0.
0/0 is not a number — it is an indeterminate form that needs a rule.

steps.title: Forms and the rule
steps.body:
Indeterminate forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰.

**L'Hôpital:** if f(x)/g(x) → 0/0 or ∞/∞ as x → a, then lim f/g = lim f′/g′, provided the latter exists. Differentiate numerator and denominator **separately** (not the quotient rule).

steps.title: Converting other forms
steps.body:
- 0·∞: write f·g = f/(1/g).
- ∞ − ∞: combine into a single fraction.
- 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰: let y = f^g, take log y = g·log f, find its limit L, then answer = e^L.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** lim (x→0) (1 − cos x)/x² = lim sin x/(2x) = lim cos x/2 = 1/2.

**Example 2.** lim (x→0) (1 + x)^(1/x) — form 1^∞. log y = log(1 + x)/x → (1/(1 + x))/1 → 1 ⇒ limit = e.

**Example 3.** lim (x→0⁺) x log x — form 0·(−∞). Write log x/(1/x) → (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the rule when the form is not 0/0 or ∞/∞ (e.g. lim (x→0) (x+1)/x).
- Using the quotient rule on f/g.
- Forgetting to exponentiate back after taking logs.

activity.prompt: Sort each limit by its indeterminate form

quiz.why: (eˣ − 1)/x is of the form 0/0. L'Hôpital gives eˣ/1 → 1.
Let y = (cos x)^(1/x²). ln y = ln cos x/x² → (−tan x)/(2x) → −1/2 by L'Hôpital, so y → e^(−1/2).
L'Hôpital's rule says the limit of f/g equals the limit of f′/g′, that is, the numerator and denominator are differentiated separately, not by the quotient rule.
options: the whole fraction by quotient rule

quiz.q: Which is NOT an indeterminate form?
quiz.why: 0/∞ is not indeterminate; it tends to 0. The others (∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0/0) are indeterminate forms.
(x − sin x)/x³ → (1 − cos x)/(3x²) → sin x/(6x) → 1/6 by repeated L'Hôpital (or from the series x³/6).

questions.q: nth derivative of e^(5x)
questions.why: d/dx e^(5x) = 5e^(5x), so the nth derivative is 5ⁿe^(5x).

questions.q: Maclaurin series is a Taylor expansion about
questions.why: A Maclaurin series is a Taylor series about a = 0.

questions.q: Which function satisfies Rolle's theorem on [0, π]?
questions.why: sin x is continuous and differentiable on [0, π] with sin 0 = sin π = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies. tan x and 1/x are not continuous on [0, π], and |x − 1| is not differentiable at 1.

questions.q: lim (x→0) sin 3x / x =
questions.why: By L'Hôpital, sin 3x/x → 3cos 3x/1 = 3 as x → 0.

questions.q: In (uv)ₙ, number of terms in Leibniz expansion is
questions.why: Leibniz's expansion (uv)ₙ = Σ ⁿC_r u_{n−r}v_r runs from r = 0 to n, which gives n + 1 terms.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For f(x) = x^(2/3) on [−1,1], Rolle's theorem cannot be applied.  Reason (R): f is not differentiable at x = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: f(−1) = f(1) = 1, but f′(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) does not exist at 0, so differentiability on (−1, 1) fails. This explains why Rolle's theorem cannot be applied.

questions.q: c of LMVT for f(x) = log x on [1, e]
questions.why: LMVT: f′(c) = 1/c = (ln e − ln 1)/(e − 1) = 1/(e − 1), so c = e − 1 ≈ 1.718, which is in (1, e).

questions.q: Coefficient of x² in Maclaurin series of log(1 + x)
questions.why: ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …, so the coefficient of x² is −1/2.
Let y = (1 + 2/x)ˣ. ln y = x ln(1 + 2/x) → 2, so y → e².

questions.q: If y = e^(ax)·x, then y₃ =
questions.why: By Leibniz with u = e^(ax) and v = x: y₃ = x·a³e^(ax) + 3·1·a²e^(ax) = a²e^(ax)(ax + 3).

questions.q: Case: A sensor's output is f(t) = t³ − 3t on [0, √3]. A student claims the rate is zero somewhere inside. Using Rolle's theorem, the instant is
questions.why: f(0) = 0 and f(√3) = 3√3 − 3√3 = 0, so Rolle applies. f′(t) = 3t² − 3 = 0 gives t = 1, which lies in (0, √3).

questions.q: lim (x→0) (1/x − 1/sin x)
questions.why: 1/x − 1/sin x = (sin x − x)/(x sin x) ≈ (−x³/6)/x² = −x/6 → 0.

questions.q: If y = sin⁻¹x, value of y₅ at x = 0 (using (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ − (2n+1)xy₍ₙ₊₁₎ − n²yₙ = 0)
questions.why: At x = 0 the recurrence reduces to y_{n+2} = n²yₙ. With y₁ = 1: y₃ = 1² × 1 = 1 and y₅ = 3² × y₃ = 9.

questions.q: Using Taylor's series, √(4.1) ≈ (2 terms after 2)
lim (x→0) (a^x − b^x)/x
questions.why: By L'Hôpital, (aˣ − bˣ)/x → aˣ ln a − bˣ ln b → ln a − ln b = ln(a/b).

courses.title: Maths I · Unit 2 · Partial differentiation and its applications
courses.summary: Partial derivatives, total derivative and chain rule, Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, Jacobians, errors, maxima–minima of two variables and Lagrange multipliers.
outcomes: Compute partial and total derivatives using the chain rule
Apply Euler's theorem and its corollaries
Evaluate Jacobians and use them for functional dependence
Find extrema with and without constraints
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Partial derivatives, total derivative and chain rule

scenes.text: Temperature on a plate is T(x,y) = 100 − x² − 2y².
An ant walks along a path x(t), y(t). How fast does the temperature it feels change? Chain rule.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: For u = f(x,y): ∂u/∂x is the derivative with y held constant; ∂u/∂y with x held constant. Higher orders: ∂²u/∂x², ∂²u/∂x∂y. For smooth functions the mixed partials are equal (∂²u/∂x∂y = ∂²u/∂y∂x).

steps.title: Total derivative and chain rule
steps.body:
If u = f(x,y), x = x(t), y = y(t): du/dt = ∂u/∂x · dx/dt + ∂u/∂y · dy/dt.
If x = x(r,s), y = y(r,s): ∂u/∂r = uₓ xᵣ + u_y yᵣ.
Implicit function f(x,y) = 0: dy/dx = −fₓ/f_y.
Total differential: du = uₓ dx + u_y dy (used for small errors).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x²y + y³, x = t², y = 2t. du/dt = (2xy)(2t) + (x² + 3y²)(2). Here 2xy = 4t³, ×2t = 8t⁴; x² + 3y² = t⁴ + 12t², ×2 = 2t⁴ + 24t². du/dt = 10t⁴ + 24t². (Check by substitution: u = 2t⁵ + 8t³ ⇒ 10t⁴ + 24t² ✔)

**Example 2.** x³ + y³ = 3axy. dy/dx = −(3x² − 3ay)/(3y² − 3ax) = (ay − x²)/(y² − ax).

**Example 3 (errors).** Area of a rectangle A = xy, x = 10 m, y = 5 m, each measured with error 0.01 m. dA = y dx + x dy = 5(0.01) + 10(0.01) = 0.15 m² (percentage 0.3%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the other variable as a function while doing ∂/∂x.
- Dropping the minus sign in dy/dx = −fₓ/f_y.
- Adding absolute errors without converting to percentage when asked for % error.

activity.prompt: u = x²y, x = 2, y = 3. If x increases by 0.01 and y by 0.02, approximate change du (= 2xy dx + x² dy).

quiz.why: Treat y as a constant: ∂/∂x(x²y³) = 2xy³.
For an implicit function f(x, y) = 0, dy/dx = −f_x/f_y.
For a function with continuous second partial derivatives, mixed partials are equal (Clairaut/Schwarz theorem).
For u = e^(xy), differentiating with respect to y treats x as constant: ∂u/∂y = x e^(xy).

quiz.q: Percentage error in A = πr² if r has 1% error
quiz.why: dA/A = 2dr/r, so a 1% error in r gives a 2% error in A = πr².

scenes.text: An economist's output Q = K^0.3 L^0.7 doubles when both inputs double.
That is homogeneity of degree 1 — Euler's theorem gives x Qₓ + y Q_y = Q.

steps.title: Homogeneous functions
steps.body:
u(x,y) is homogeneous of degree n if u(tx, ty) = tⁿ u(x,y), equivalently u = xⁿ φ(y/x).

**Euler:** x ∂u/∂x + y ∂u/∂y = n u.
**Corollary:** x²uₓₓ + 2xy uₓᵧ + y²u_yy = n(n − 1)u.

steps.title: When u itself is not homogeneous
steps.body:
If f(u) is homogeneous of degree n, then x uₓ + y u_y = n f(u)/f′(u) = g(u).
Second order: x²uₓₓ + 2xy uₓᵧ + y²u_yy = g(u)[g′(u) − 1].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x³ + y³ + 3x²y: degree 3 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y = 3u. (Check: x(3x² + 6xy) + y(3y² + 3x²) = 3x³ + 9x²y + 3y³ = 3u ✔)

**Example 2.** u = sin⁻¹[(x² + y²)/(x + y)]. sin u is homogeneous of degree 1 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y = sin u/cos u = tan u.

**Example 3.** For Example 2, second order: g = tan u, g′ = sec²u ⇒ x²uₓₓ + 2xyuₓᵧ + y²u_yy = tan u (sec²u − 1) = tan³u.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a function homogeneous when terms have different degrees (x² + y).
- Forgetting n(n − 1) in the second-order corollary.
- Applying Euler to u directly when only sin u or tan u is homogeneous.

quiz.why: u = x⁴ + y⁴ is homogeneous of degree 4, so Euler's theorem gives x u_x + y u_y = 4u.
tan⁻¹(y/x) is homogeneous of degree 0, so by Euler x u_x + y u_y = 0·u = 0.

quiz.q: If u is homogeneous of degree 3, x²uₓₓ + 2xyuₓᵧ + y²u_yy =
quiz.why: For a homogeneous function of degree n, x²u_xx + 2xy u_xy + y²u_yy = n(n − 1)u. With n = 3 this is 6u.

quiz.q: u = log[(x² + y²)/(x + y)]: e^u homogeneous of degree 1 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y =
quiz.why: e^u = (x² + y²)/(x + y) is homogeneous of degree 1. For f = e^u, x u_x + y u_y = n f/f′ = e^u/e^u = 1.
A homogeneous function has all terms of the same degree. x² has degree 2 but 3y has degree 1, so it is not homogeneous.

scenes.text: Kabir integrates over a circular disc and switches to polar coordinates.
The factor r in dx dy = r dr dθ is a Jacobian.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
J = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) = det[[uₓ, u_y],[vₓ, v_y]].
- Chain: ∂(u,v)/∂(r,s) = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) · ∂(x,y)/∂(r,s)
- Inverse: J · J′ = 1 where J′ = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)
- **Functional dependence:** u, v are functionally related (dependent) iff J = 0 identically.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. ∂(x,y)/∂(r,θ) = cos θ·r cos θ − (−r sin θ)·sin θ = r.

**Example 2.** Spherical: x = r sinθ cosφ, y = r sinθ sinφ, z = r cosθ ⇒ ∂(x,y,z)/∂(r,θ,φ) = r² sin θ.

**Example 3.** u = x + y, v = xy. J = det[[1,1],[y,x]] = x − y; so ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) = 1/(x − y).

steps.title: Testing dependence
steps.body: **Example 4.** u = (x + y)/(1 − xy), v = tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y. Compute J: uₓ = (1 + y²)/(1 − xy)², u_y = (1 + x²)/(1 − xy)², vₓ = 1/(1 + x²), v_y = 1/(1 + y²). J = [(1+y²)/(1+y²) − (1+x²)/(1+x²)]/(1 − xy)² = 0 ⇒ dependent. Indeed u = tan v.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping rows/columns inconsistently (changes the sign).
- Forgetting |J| (absolute value) when changing variables in integrals.
- Concluding dependence from J = 0 at a single point — it must vanish identically.

activity.prompt: Match the transformation with its Jacobian
pairs: u = x + y, v = x − y

quiz.why: For x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ the Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r.
The Jacobians of inverse transformations are reciprocals: J·J′ = 1, so J′ = 1/4.

quiz.q: u, v are functionally dependent iff J is
quiz.why: Two functions are functionally dependent exactly when their Jacobian vanishes identically.
For spherical coordinates the Jacobian ∂(x, y, z)/∂(r, θ, φ) = r² sin θ.

lessons.title: Maxima and minima of functions of two variables

scenes.text: A packaging engineer wants the open box of volume 32 cm³ with the least cardboard.
That is minimising S(x,y) — critical points plus the second-derivative test.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Solve fₓ = 0, f_y = 0 for critical points.
2. At each, r = fₓₓ, s = fₓᵧ, t = f_yy.
3. rt − s² > 0 and r < 0 ⇒ **maximum**; rt − s² > 0 and r > 0 ⇒ **minimum**; rt − s² < 0 ⇒ **saddle point**; rt − s² = 0 ⇒ further investigation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** f = x³ + y³ − 3axy (a > 0). fₓ = 3x² − 3ay = 0, f_y = 3y² − 3ax = 0 ⇒ (0,0), (a,a).
r = 6x, s = −3a, t = 6y.
At (0,0): rt − s² = −9a² < 0 ⇒ saddle.
At (a,a): 36a² − 9a² > 0, r = 6a > 0 ⇒ minimum, f = −a³.

**Example 2.** Open box volume 32: S = xy + 64/x + 64/y (with z = 32/(xy), S = xy + 2xz + 2yz). Sₓ = y − 64/x² = 0, S_y = x − 64/y² = 0 ⇒ x = y = 4, z = 2. r = 128/x³ = 2 > 0, rt − s² = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 ⇒ minimum, S = 48 cm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding max/min from fₓ = f_y = 0 alone.
- Using rt − s² with s = fₓ instead of fₓᵧ.
- Ignoring points where the test is inconclusive.

quiz.why: At a critical point, if rt − s² > 0 and r < 0, the function has a local maximum.
If rt − s² < 0 at a critical point, it is a saddle point (neither max nor min).

quiz.why: For f = x² − y², r = 2, t = −2, s = 0, so rt − s² = −4 < 0, a saddle at the origin.
At (2, −3), f = 4 + 9 − 8 − 18 = −13, a minimum since rt − s² = 4 > 0 and r > 0.

scenes.text: A satellite dish feed must lie on the paraboloid while minimising distance to a point.
When a constraint links the variables, Lagrange multipliers turn it into an unconstrained system.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Extremise f(x,y,z) subject to φ(x,y,z) = 0.
Form F = f + λφ. Solve Fₓ = 0, F_y = 0, F_z = 0 together with φ = 0. The solutions are the stationary points; the nature is usually decided from the physical problem.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Maximise xyz subject to x + y + z = 12.
F = xyz + λ(x + y + z − 12): yz + λ = 0, xz + λ = 0, xy + λ = 0 ⇒ yz = xz = xy ⇒ x = y = z = 4, max = 64.

**Example 2.** Minimise x² + y² + z² subject to x + y + z = 3a.
2x + λ = 0 etc. ⇒ x = y = z = a, min = 3a².

**Example 3.** Rectangular box of volume V with least surface: by symmetry and Lagrange, x = y = z = V^(1/3) (a cube).

steps.title: Shortcut checks
steps.body: Symmetric functions with symmetric constraints usually have the extremum at equal variables — use this to check your answer, not to replace the working in an exam.

steps.title: Common mistakes

questions.why: f_x = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1 and f_y = 2y = 0 gives y = 0. The stationary points are (1, 0) and (−1, 0).

questions.why: The Jacobian is the determinant of [[1 − v, −u], [v, u]] = u(1 − v) + uv = u.

questions.why: sin u = (x + y)/(√x + √y) is homogeneous of degree 1/2. Then x u_x + y u_y = (1/2) sin u/cos u = (1/2) tan u.

questions.q: Case: Temperature T = 400xyz² on the sphere x² + y² + z² = 1. Using Lagrange, the highest temperature is
questions.why: By Lagrange multipliers x² = y² = 1/4 and z² = 1/2 give the extremum: T = 400 × (1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 50.

questions.why: For u = f(y − z, z − x, x − y), the partial derivatives contributed by the arguments cancel in pairs in u_x + u_y + u_z, so the sum is 0.

questions.why: The Jacobian = x_u y_v − x_v y_u = e^u cos v × e^u cos v + e^u sin v × e^u sin v = e^(2u)(cos²v + sin²v) = e^(2u).

steps.title: Evaluating ∬
steps.body:
∬_R f dx dy over R: integrate the inner variable between its curve limits, then the outer between constants.

**Change of order:** sketch the region, then re-describe it with horizontal strips instead of vertical ones (or vice versa) and write new limits.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∫₀¹∫₀^x (x² + y²) dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x³ + x³/3) dx = ∫₀¹ (4/3)x³ dx = 1/3.

**Example 2.** Change order and evaluate ∫₀^∞∫ₓ^∞ (e^(−y)/y) dy dx.
Region: 0 ≤ x ≤ y < ∞. New order: y from 0 to ∞, x from 0 to y.
∫₀^∞ (e^(−y)/y)·y dy = ∫₀^∞ e^(−y) dy = 1.

**Example 3.** Area between y = x² and y = x: ∫₀¹∫_(x²)^x dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/6.

steps.title: Sketch first
steps.body: Mark intersection points of the boundary curves. A vertical strip (dy inner) has y from lower curve to upper curve; a horizontal strip (dx inner) has x from left curve to right curve.

steps.title: Common mistakes

courses.summary: Rank by echelon/normal form, consistency of linear systems, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, Cayley–Hamilton theorem, diagonalisation and quadratic forms.

scenes.text: Vikram has 4 sensor equations but suspects only 3 carry new information.
The rank of the coefficient matrix tells him exactly how many are independent.

steps.title: Definition and methods
steps.body:
Rank ρ(A) = order of the largest non-vanishing minor = number of non-zero rows in row-echelon form = number of linearly independent rows (or columns).

Elementary row operations (swap, scale by non-zero, add a multiple of another row) do not change rank.

steps.title: Useful facts
steps.body:
- ρ(A) ≤ min(m, n) for m × n A.
- ρ(A) = n for an n × n matrix iff det A ≠ 0 (non-singular).
- ρ(AB) ≤ min(ρ(A), ρ(B)).
- Normal form [[Iᵣ, 0],[0, 0]] has rank r.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using column operations while solving equations (fine for rank only).
- Stopping before the matrix is fully in echelon form.
- Arithmetic slips — always check with a determinant when the matrix is square.

quiz.why: The 3 × 3 identity matrix is non-singular, with 3 independent rows, so its rank is 3.

quiz.q: Rank of a non-zero 3×4 matrix is at most
quiz.why: Rank cannot exceed the smaller of the number of rows and columns, so a 3 × 4 matrix has rank at most 3.
Elementary row operations do not change the rank of a matrix.

quiz.q: If det A = 0 for 3×3 A, rank is
quiz.why: If det A = 0 the matrix is singular and cannot have full rank, so its rank is less than 3.
The second row is half the first, so there is only one independent row and the rank is 1.

scenes.text: Flow balance at four junctions gives four equations in four unknown flows.
Is there a unique answer, many, or none? Compare ρ(A) and ρ([A|B]).

steps.title: Consistency (Rouché–Capelli)
steps.body:
For AX = B with n unknowns:
- ρ(A) ≠ ρ([A|B]) ⇒ inconsistent (no solution)
- ρ(A) = ρ([A|B]) = n ⇒ unique solution
- ρ(A) = ρ([A|B]) = r < n ⇒ infinitely many solutions with n − r free parameters.
Homogeneous AX = 0 is always consistent; non-trivial solutions exist iff ρ(A) < n (det A = 0 for square A).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1.
[A|B] → R₂ − R₁: [0,−2,0 | −4] ⇒ y = 2; R₃ − 2R₁: [0,−1,−3 | −11] ⇒ −2 − 3z = −11 ⇒ z = 3; x = 1. Unique: (1, 2, 3).

**Example 2.** For what λ, μ does x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + λz = μ have (i) no, (ii) unique, (iii) infinite solutions?
Reduce: R₂ − R₁ = [0,1,2|4], R₃ − R₂ = [0,0,λ−3 | μ−10].
(i) λ = 3, μ ≠ 10; (ii) λ ≠ 3; (iii) λ = 3, μ = 10.

steps.title: Gauss elimination vs Gauss–Jordan
steps.body: Gauss elimination stops at upper-triangular form and back-substitutes; Gauss–Jordan continues to reduced form so the answer reads off directly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing ρ(A) with n only, ignoring the augmented matrix.
- Forgetting that a homogeneous system always has the trivial solution.
- Sign errors during back-substitution.

quiz.why: By the Rouché–Capelli theorem, AX = B is consistent when the rank of A equals the rank of the augmented matrix [A|B].

quiz.q: Homogeneous system with 3 unknowns, ρ(A) = 2, has
quiz.why: A homogeneous system with n = 3 unknowns and rank 2 has n − r = 1 free parameter, so infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Square homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions iff
quiz.why: A square homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions exactly when det A = 0, i.e. the rank is less than n.

quiz.q: Solution of x + y = 3, x − y = 1
quiz.why: Adding the equations gives 2x = 4, so x = 2. Then y = 1.
For λ = 3 and μ = 10 the ranks of the coefficient and augmented matrices are both 2, which is less than 3 unknowns, so there are infinitely many solutions.

scenes.text: A footbridge's vibration modes are eigenvectors of its stiffness–mass matrix.
The eigenvalues give the squared natural frequencies — the bridge must not resonate with footsteps.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
AX = λX, X ≠ 0. Characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0. For 3×3: λ³ − (tr A)λ² + (sum of principal 2×2 minors)λ − det A = 0.
Eigenvectors: solve (A − λI)X = 0 for each λ.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Σλᵢ = trace A, Πλᵢ = det A.
- Eigenvalues of A⁻¹ are 1/λ; of Aᵏ are λᵏ; of kA are kλ.
- Triangular matrix: eigenvalues are diagonal entries.
- Real symmetric matrix: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct λ.
- A and Aᵀ have the same eigenvalues.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the eigenvector as the zero vector.
- Sign error in the λ² coefficient of the 3×3 characteristic polynomial.
- Assuming every matrix has n independent eigenvectors.

quiz.why: The sum of the eigenvalues of a matrix equals its trace.
The eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, 2 and 5.

quiz.q: If λ is an eigenvalue of A, eigenvalue of A⁻¹ is
quiz.why: If AX = λX then A⁻¹X = (1/λ)X, so 1/λ is an eigenvalue of A⁻¹.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are
quiz.why: The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are always real.

quiz.q: A singular matrix has an eigenvalue
quiz.why: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues. A singular matrix has det = 0, so one eigenvalue must be 0.

scenes.text: A population model needs A¹⁰ of a 2×2 transition matrix.
Diagonalisation turns A¹⁰ into P D¹⁰ P⁻¹ — just powers of numbers.

steps.title: Cayley–Hamilton
steps.body:
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If |A − λI| = λ² − 5λ + 6, then A² − 5A + 6I = 0.
Uses: A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/6 from multiplying by A⁻¹; higher powers reduce to combinations of I and A.

steps.title: Diagonalisation and quadratic forms
steps.body:
If A has n independent eigenvectors, P = [X₁ … Xₙ] gives P⁻¹AP = D = diag(λᵢ) and Aᵏ = P Dᵏ P⁻¹. For symmetric A use orthonormal eigenvectors: Pᵀ A P = D (orthogonal reduction).
Quadratic form Q = XᵀAX: positive definite if all λ > 0; negative definite if all λ < 0; indefinite if mixed signs. Rank = number of non-zero λ, index = number of positive λ, signature = (positive − negative).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the constant term as a number instead of a multiple of I.
- Putting eigenvectors in P in a different order from the λ in D.
- Using off-diagonal entries of A for the quadratic form without halving the xy coefficient.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to find A⁻¹ by Cayley–Hamilton
items: Replace λ by A and constants by multiples of I
Solve for A⁻¹ and verify A·A⁻¹ = I

quiz.why: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem says that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation.

quiz.q: P⁻¹AP = D where columns of P are
quiz.why: In P⁻¹AP = D, the columns of P are the eigenvectors of A, and D has the eigenvalues on its diagonal.
Q = x² + y² + z² has matrix I with all eigenvalues 1 > 0, so it is positive definite.
The symmetric matrix of a quadratic form has half the cross-term coefficient off the diagonal: 4xy gives 2 and 2, so [[1, 2], [2, 1]].

questions.q: Rank of zero matrix
questions.why: The zero matrix has no non-zero minor, so its rank is 0.

questions.q: Eigenvalues of [[5,3],[0,−2]]
questions.why: The matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are the diagonal entries: 5 and −2.

questions.q: Trace of A equals
questions.why: The trace (sum of diagonal entries) equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
If the ranks of A and [A|B] are equal and equal to the number of unknowns, the system has a unique solution.

questions.why: If Ax = λx then A²x = λ²x, so the eigenvalues of A² are 1, 4 and 9.

questions.why: The characteristic equation is λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0. Here trace 5 and det = 4 − 6 = −2, so λ² − 5λ − 2 = 0.

Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: Nature of Q = x² − y²
questions.why: Q = x² − y² has matrix diag(1, −1) with eigenvalues 1 and −1, so it takes both signs: indefinite.

questions.q: For which k does kx + y = 0, x + ky = 0 have non-trivial solution?
questions.why: The determinant of [[k, 1], [1, k]] is k² − 1. Non-trivial solutions exist only if it is zero, so k = ±1.

questions.q: If A² − 3A + 2I = 0, A³ in terms of A and I
questions.why: A² = 3A − 2I. Then A³ = 3A² − 2A = 3(3A − 2I) − 2A = 7A − 6I.

questions.why: (A − 3I)X = 0 gives −x + y = 0, i.e. x = y, so (1, 1) is an eigenvector.

questions.why: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues: 2 × 3 × λ = 24, so λ = 4.
All rows are multiples of the first row, so there is only one independent row and the rank is 1.
The second equation's left side is twice the first, but 5 ≠ 2 × 2. The rank of A is 1 and the rank of [A|B] is 2, so the system is inconsistent.

questions.q: If A = [[1,2],[2,1]], A⁵ via Cayley–Hamilton has eigenvalues
questions.why: The eigenvalues of A are 3 and −1 (trace 2, det −3). Those of A⁵ are 3⁵ = 243 and (−1)⁵ = −1.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Eigenvalues of an orthogonal matrix have modulus 1.  Reason (R): An orthogonal matrix preserves vector length.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

questions.why: Both true: an orthogonal matrix preserves length, ‖AX‖ = ‖X‖. If AX = λX, then |λ|‖X‖ = ‖X‖, so |λ| = 1. The reason explains the assertion.

courses.summary: Convergence of sequences and series, comparison, ratio, root and integral tests, alternating series and absolute convergence, and power series with radius of convergence.
outcomes: Decide convergence of sequences and standard series
Choose and apply comparison, ratio, root and integral tests

lessons.title: Sequences and the basics of series

scenes.text: Walk half the distance to a wall, then half the rest, and so on.
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … — infinitely many steps, yet a finite total of 1.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A sequence aₙ converges to L if aₙ → L as n → ∞. A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ converge.

**nth-term test:** if Σaₙ converges then aₙ → 0. So if aₙ ↛ 0, the series diverges. (aₙ → 0 alone does NOT guarantee convergence.)

steps.title: Two benchmark series
steps.body:
- Geometric Σ rⁿ converges iff |r| < 1, sum a/(1 − r) from first term a.
- p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges iff p > 1. Harmonic series (p = 1) diverges.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** aₙ = (2n + 1)/(3n − 1) → 2/3 (divide by n). Converges to 2/3.

**Example 2.** Σ n/(n + 1) diverges since aₙ → 1 ≠ 0.

**Example 3.** Σ 3/2ⁿ (n ≥ 1) = 3·(1/2)/(1 − 1/2) = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding convergence of Σaₙ just because aₙ → 0 (harmonic series counter-example).
- Using the geometric sum formula when |r| ≥ 1.
- Confusing the sequence limit with the series sum.

quiz.why: Σ1/n^1.5 is a p-series with p = 1.5 > 1, so it converges.
This is a geometric series with first term 1 and ratio 1/3, so the sum is 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2.
(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e as n → ∞. This is the standard definition of e.
The nth-term test says that if aₙ does not tend to 0 then the series diverges. But aₙ → 0 does not prove convergence, so it can prove divergence only.
Σ2ⁿ is a geometric series with common ratio r = 2 ≥ 1, so it diverges (its terms grow without limit).

lessons.title: Comparison, ratio, root and integral tests

scenes.text: Faced with Σ n²/3ⁿ, Pooja wonders which test to use.
Powers like 3ⁿ or factorials scream 'ratio test'.

steps.title: Tests for positive-term series
steps.body:
- **Limit comparison:** if aₙ/bₙ → finite non-zero l, Σaₙ and Σbₙ behave alike (pick bₙ = 1/nᵖ from leading powers).
- **D'Alembert ratio:** aₙ₊₁/aₙ → l: l < 1 converges, l > 1 diverges, l = 1 test fails.
- **Cauchy root:** (aₙ)^(1/n) → l, same conclusion.
- **Integral test:** f positive decreasing, Σf(n) and ∫₁^∞ f(x)dx converge together.
- **Raabe's test** (when ratio gives 1): n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁ − 1) → k, k > 1 converges, k < 1 diverges.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ n²/3ⁿ: ratio = ((n+1)²/n²)(1/3) → 1/3 < 1 ⇒ converges.

**Example 2.** Σ (2n + 3)/(n³ + 1): compare with 1/n²; ratio → 2 ⇒ converges.

**Example 3.** Σ (n/(n + 1))^(n²): root test (n/(n+1))ⁿ → 1/e < 1 ⇒ converges.

**Example 4.** Σ 1/(n log n): ∫ dx/(x log x) = log log x → ∞ ⇒ diverges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring convergence when the ratio limit equals 1.
- Using comparison with a series that goes the wrong way (larger divergent series proves nothing).
- Forgetting the integral test needs f decreasing.

quiz.why: By the ratio test, if the limit of aₙ₊₁/aₙ is l < 1, the series converges. Here l = 1/2 < 1.
For large n, 1/(n² + n) behaves like 1/n². By comparison with the convergent Σ1/n² (p = 2), the series converges.
The ratio of consecutive terms of n!/10ⁿ is (n + 1)/10, which tends to infinity. Since l > 1, the series diverges.
For Σ1/n² the ratio (n/(n + 1))² → 1, so the ratio test is inconclusive. We need the p-series test instead.
Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges.

scenes.text: 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converges to log 2, though 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges.
Convergence that depends on cancelling signs is called conditional.

steps.title: Leibniz test
steps.body:
Σ (−1)^(n+1) uₙ with uₙ > 0 converges if (i) uₙ ≥ uₙ₊₁ eventually and (ii) uₙ → 0.

**Absolute convergence:** Σ|aₙ| converges ⇒ Σaₙ converges. If Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it is **conditionally** convergent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ (−1)^(n+1)/n: uₙ = 1/n decreasing → 0 ⇒ converges; Σ1/n diverges ⇒ conditionally convergent.

**Example 2.** Σ (−1)ⁿ/n²: Σ1/n² converges ⇒ absolutely convergent.

**Example 3.** Σ (−1)ⁿ n/(n + 1): uₙ → 1 ≠ 0 ⇒ diverges (oscillates).

steps.title: Error bound
steps.body: For a Leibniz series, the error after stopping at term n is at most uₙ₊₁ — handy for 'how many terms for 3-decimal accuracy?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the 'decreasing' check.
- Saying 'absolutely convergent' for the alternating harmonic series.
- Forgetting that absolute convergence implies convergence (not the reverse).

quiz.q: Leibniz test requires uₙ to be
quiz.why: The Leibniz (alternating series) test needs the terms uₙ to decrease and tend to 0.
The Leibniz test shows that Σ(−1)ⁿ/√n converges. But Σ1/√n diverges, so convergence is conditional, not absolute.
If a series converges absolutely (Σ|aₙ| converges), then it converges. The reverse is not always true.
ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … converges at x = 1, so 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … = ln 2 (log 2).

quiz.q: Terms needed so error < 0.01 in Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n
quiz.why: The error is less than the first neglected term. We need 1/(n + 1) < 0.01, so n is about 100.

lessons.title: Power series and radius of convergence

scenes.text: The series 1 + x + x² + … equals 1/(1 − x) — but only for |x| < 1.
Every power series has a radius inside which it converges.

steps.title: Radius of convergence
steps.body: For Σ aₙ xⁿ: R = lim |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| (if it exists) or 1/R = lim |aₙ|^(1/n). The series converges absolutely for |x| < R and diverges for |x| > R. Check the end points x = ±R separately.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ xⁿ/n: R = lim (n+1)/n = 1. At x = 1: harmonic (diverges); at x = −1: alternating harmonic (converges). Interval [−1, 1).

**Example 2.** Σ xⁿ/n!: R = lim (n + 1) = ∞ — converges for all x (it is eˣ).

**Example 3.** Σ n!xⁿ: R = lim 1/(n + 1) = 0 — converges only at x = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to test the end points.
- Inverting the ratio (using aₙ₊₁/aₙ for R).
- Confusing radius with interval.

activity.prompt: Radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/3ⁿ

quiz.why: For Σxⁿ/n!, the ratio |x|/(n + 1) → 0 for every x, so the radius of convergence is infinite.
R = 1. At x = 1 the series is the harmonic series, which diverges, and at x = −1 it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges. So the interval is [−1, 1).
The ratio of coefficients (n + 1)/n → 1, so the radius of convergence of Σnxⁿ is 1.
For Σn!xⁿ the ratio (n + 1)|x| → ∞ for any x ≠ 0, so the radius is 0 and it converges only at x = 0.
Σ(2x)ⁿ is geometric in 2x and converges when |2x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2.

questions.q: Σ 1/n diverges. This is the
questions.why: Σ1/n is the harmonic series, which diverges.

questions.q: Σ (1/2)ⁿ from n = 0 equals
questions.why: A geometric series with first term 1 and ratio 1/2 has sum 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2.

questions.q: p-series converges iff
questions.why: A p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges only when p > 1.

questions.q: Σ (n + 1)/n is
questions.why: (n + 1)/n → 1, not 0, so by the nth-term test the series diverges.

questions.q: Σ 1/(n(n + 1)) equals
questions.why: 1/(n(n + 1)) = 1/n − 1/(n + 1). The series telescopes, so the sum is 1.

questions.q: Ratio test on Σ 2ⁿ/n! gives
questions.why: The ratio of consecutive terms of Σ2ⁿ/n! is 2/(n + 1) → 0 < 1, so the series converges.

questions.q: Σ (−1)ⁿ/n is
questions.why: The Leibniz test shows Σ(−1)ⁿ/n converges, but Σ1/n diverges, so it is conditionally convergent.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Σ 1/n^(1.01) converges.  Reason (R): Every p-series with p > 1 converges.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: 1.01 > 1, and every p-series with p > 1 converges, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n²
questions.why: The ratio of coefficients n²/(n + 1)² → 1, so the radius of convergence is 1.

questions.q: Σ (n/(2n + 1))ⁿ by root test
questions.why: By the root test the nth root of (n/(2n + 1))ⁿ is n/(2n + 1) → 1/2 < 1, so the series converges.

questions.q: Σ 1/(n (log n)²), n ≥ 2
questions.why: By the integral test, ∫dx/(x ln²x) = −1/ln x converges, so the series converges.

questions.q: Interval of convergence of Σ (x − 2)ⁿ/n
questions.why: The ratio gives |x − 2| < 1, i.e. 1 < x < 3. At x = 1 the series is alternating harmonic (converges); at x = 3 it is harmonic (diverges). So the interval is [1, 3).

questions.q: Case: A damped spring's total travel is 10 + 10(0.8) + 10(0.8)² + … cm. Total =
questions.why: The total travel is a geometric series with first term 10 and ratio 0.8: 10/(1 − 0.8) = 50 cm.

questions.q: Σ nⁿ/n! (use ratio)
questions.why: The ratio of consecutive terms of Σnⁿ/n! is (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e > 1, so the series diverges.

questions.q: Σ 1·3·5…(2n−1)/(2·4·6…2n) — ratio gives 1; Raabe's gives k = 1/2 so the series
questions.why: When the ratio test gives 1, Raabe's test applies. If k < 1 the series diverges. Here k = 1/2 < 1, so it diverges.

steps.title: Order, degree, separable form
steps.body:
Order = highest derivative; degree = power of that derivative after clearing radicals/fractions.
**Variable separable:** dy/dx = f(x)g(y) ⇒ ∫dy/g(y) = ∫f(x)dx + C.

steps.title: Homogeneous equations
steps.body: dy/dx = f(x,y)/g(x,y) where f, g are homogeneous of the same degree. Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, then separate v and x.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** dy/dx = xy². ∫y^(−2)dy = ∫x dx ⇒ −1/y = x²/2 + C.

**Example 2.** (x² + y²)dx − 2xy dy = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(2xy). Put y = vx: v + xv′ = (1 + v²)/(2v) ⇒ xv′ = (1 − v²)/(2v) ⇒ ∫2v/(1 − v²) dv = ∫dx/x ⇒ −log(1 − v²) = log x + c ⇒ x(1 − y²/x²) = C ⇒ x² − y² = Cx.

steps.title: Initial-value problem
steps.body: **Example 3.** dy/dx = y cos x, y(0) = 2. log y = sin x + c, y = Ae^(sin x); y(0) = A = 2 ⇒ y = 2e^(sin x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Losing solutions when dividing by g(y) (e.g. y = 0 is also a solution of y′ = xy²).
- Forgetting the constant of integration until the end, then not applying the initial condition.
- Substituting y = vx but not replacing dy/dx by v + x dv/dx.

scenes.text: A hiker's altitude is φ(x,y). Small changes satisfy dφ = φₓdx + φ_ydy = 0 along a contour.
If M dx + N dy is such a total differential, the ODE is exact.

steps.title: Test and solution
steps.body:
M dx + N dy = 0 is exact iff ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x.
Solution: ∫M dx (treating y constant) + ∫(terms of N free of x) dy = C.

steps.title: Integrating factor rules
steps.body:
- (Mᵧ − Nₓ)/N = f(x) ⇒ IF = e^(∫f dx)
- (Nₓ − Mᵧ)/M = g(y) ⇒ IF = e^(∫g dy)
- M, N homogeneous and Mx + Ny ≠ 0 ⇒ IF = 1/(Mx + Ny)
- Equation of form y f(xy)dx + x g(xy)dy = 0 ⇒ IF = 1/(Mx − Ny)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** (2xy + 3)dx + (x² − 1)dy = 0. Mᵧ = 2x = Nₓ ⇒ exact. ∫M dx = x²y + 3x; N-terms free of x: −1 ⇒ −y. Solution: x²y + 3x − y = C.

**Example 2.** (x²+y²+x)dx + xy dy = 0. Mᵧ = 2y, Nₓ = y; (Mᵧ − Nₓ)/N = y/(xy) = 1/x ⇒ IF = x. New: (x³ + xy² + x²)dx + x²y dy = 0 (exact). Solution: x⁴/4 + x²y²/2 + x³/3 = C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Integrating N with respect to y including the x-terms again (double counting).
- Checking Mₓ = N_y instead of Mᵧ = Nₓ.
- Forgetting to multiply the whole equation by the integrating factor.

steps.title: Linear equation
steps.body:
dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x). IF = e^(∫P dx). Solution: y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.
**Bernoulli:** dy/dx + Py = Qyⁿ (n ≠ 0, 1). Divide by yⁿ and put z = y^(1−n): dz/dx + (1 − n)Pz = (1 − n)Q (linear in z).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** dy/dx + y/x = x². IF = x. yx = ∫x³dx = x⁴/4 + C ⇒ y = x³/4 + C/x.

**Example 2.** RL: di/dt + (R/L)i = E/L, i(0) = 0. IF = e^(Rt/L). i e^(Rt/L) = (E/R)e^(Rt/L) + C ⇒ C = −E/R ⇒ i = (E/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)).

**Example 3.** dy/dx + y = xy³. Divide y³: y^(−3)y′ + y^(−2) = x. z = y^(−2), z′ = −2y^(−3)y′ ⇒ z′ − 2z = −2x. IF = e^(−2x): z e^(−2x) = ∫−2x e^(−2x)dx = (x + ½)e^(−2x) + C ⇒ 1/y² = x + ½ + Ce^(2x).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using IF = e^(∫Q dx) instead of e^(∫P dx).
- Not writing the equation in standard form (coefficient of dy/dx must be 1).
- In Bernoulli, forgetting the (1 − n) factor on both terms.

steps.title: Standard models

steps.body:

40 = 60e^(−10k) ⇒ e^(−10k) = 2/3. After 20 min: T = 20 + 60(2/3)² = 20 + 26.67 = 46.7 °C.

scenes.text: A shock absorber obeys m x″ + c x′ + k x = 0.
Whether the car bounces or settles smoothly depends on the roots of mD² + cD + k = 0.

steps.title: Auxiliary equation
steps.body:
Write f(D)y = 0 with D = d/dx. Solve f(m) = 0.
- Real distinct m₁, m₂: y = c₁e^(m₁x) + c₂e^(m₂x)
- Repeated m: y = (c₁ + c₂x)e^(mx)
- Complex α ± iβ: y = e^(αx)(c₁cos βx + c₂ sin βx)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y″ − 5y′ + 6y = 0: m² − 5m + 6 = 0 ⇒ m = 2, 3 ⇒ y = c₁e^(2x) + c₂e^(3x).

**Example 2.** y″ + 4y′ + 4y = 0: (m + 2)² ⇒ y = (c₁ + c₂x)e^(−2x).

**Example 3.** y″ + 2y′ + 5y = 0: m = −1 ± 2i ⇒ y = e^(−x)(c₁cos 2x + c₂ sin 2x).

steps.title: Higher order
steps.body: (D⁴ − 1)y = 0: m = ±1, ±i ⇒ y = c₁eˣ + c₂e^(−x) + c₃cos x + c₄sin x. A triple root m gives (c₁ + c₂x + c₃x²)e^(mx).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing c₁e^(mx) + c₂e^(mx) for a repeated root (only one independent function).
- Using e^(βx) instead of cos βx, sin βx for complex roots.
- Forgetting the e^(αx) factor when α ≠ 0.

quiz.why: The auxiliary equation m² − 1 = 0 gives m = ±1, so the CF is c₁eˣ + c₂e^(−x).
m² + 9 = 0 gives m = ±3i, so the CF is c₁cos 3x + c₂sin 3x.
For a repeated root m = −1 the solution is (c₁ + c₂x)e^(−x), the second solution having an extra factor x.

steps.title: Rules (PI = X/f(D))
steps.body:
- X = e^(ax): PI = e^(ax)/f(a) if f(a) ≠ 0; if f(a) = 0, PI = x e^(ax)/f′(a).
- X = sin ax or cos ax: replace D² by −a²; if that gives zero, multiply by x and differentiate the denominator.
- X = xᵐ: expand [f(D)]⁻¹ as a power series in D up to Dᵐ.
- X = e^(ax)V: PI = e^(ax)·V/f(D + a).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** (D² − 3D + 2)y = e^(3x). PI = e^(3x)/(9 − 9 + 2) = e^(3x)/2.

**Example 2.** (D² + 4)y = sin x. PI = sin x/(−1 + 4) = (sin x)/3.

**Example 3 (resonance).** (D² + 4)y = cos 2x: D² → −4 gives 0. PI = x·cos 2x/(2D) = (x/2)·(sin 2x/2) = (x sin 2x)/4.

**Example 4.** (D² + D)y = x: PI = (1/D)(1 + D)⁻¹x = (1/D)(1 − D + …)x = (1/D)(x − 1) = x²/2 − x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 'multiply by x' rule in the failure case.
- Replacing D (not D²) by −a² for trig inputs — first reduce odd powers of D.
- Expanding (1 + D)⁻¹ beyond the degree needed or with wrong signs.

quiz.why: PI = e^(2x)/f(2) with f(D) = D² + 1, f(2) = 5.
Replace D² by −4: PI = sin 2x/(−4 + 9) = (sin 2x)/5.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
For y″ + P y′ + Q y = X with CF c₁y₁ + c₂y₂:
W = y₁y₂′ − y₂y₁′ (Wronskian).
PI = −y₁∫(y₂X/W)dx + y₂∫(y₁X/W)dx.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y″ + y = sec x. y₁ = cos x, y₂ = sin x, W = 1.
PI = −cos x∫sin x sec x dx + sin x∫cos x sec x dx = cos x·log|cos x| + x sin x.

**Example 2.** y″ + y = tan x: PI = −cos x∫sin x tan x dx + sin x∫cos x tan x dx. ∫sin²x/cos x dx = log|sec x + tan x| − sin x; ∫sin x dx = −cos x. PI = −cos x(log|sec x + tan x| − sin x) − sin x cos x = −cos x·log|sec x + tan x|.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Coefficient of y″ must be 1 before you read off X. Always compute W carefully — it is usually a constant or simple function.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign of the first term (it is −y₁∫y₂X/W).
- Using X before dividing the equation by the coefficient of y″.
- Dropping absolute values inside logs.

steps.title: Cauchy–Euler
steps.body:
x²y″ + a x y′ + b y = X(x). Put x = eᶻ, θ = d/dz: xD = θ, x²D² = θ(θ − 1). Solve in z, then z = log x.
Legendre's form (ax + b)ⁿ: put ax + b = eᶻ, (ax + b)D = aθ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x²y″ − xy′ + y = 0 ⇒ θ(θ − 1) − θ + 1 = (θ − 1)² ⇒ y = (c₁ + c₂ log x)x.

**Example 2.** x²y″ + xy′ − 4y = x²: θ² − 4 ⇒ CF c₁x² + c₂x^(−2). PI = e^(2z)/(θ² − 4) — failure: z e^(2z)/(2θ) at θ = 2 ⇒ ze^(2z)/4 = (x² log x)/4.

courses.title: Maths II · Unit 3 · Laplace transform
courses.summary: Definition and standard transforms, shifting theorems, transforms of derivatives and integrals, multiplication by t and division by t, unit step and periodic functions, inverse transforms, convolution and solving IVPs.
outcomes: Compute Laplace transforms using properties
Handle unit-step, impulse and periodic inputs
Find inverse transforms by partial fractions and convolution
Solve initial-value problems in one pass

scenes.text: At t = 0 a switch closes. Initial conditions matter, and the input may switch on and off.
The Laplace transform turns calculus in t into algebra in s and builds in initial conditions.

steps.title: Definition and table
steps.body:
L{f(t)} = F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−st)f(t)dt.
- L{1} = 1/s; L{tⁿ} = n!/s^(n+1)
- L{e^(at)} = 1/(s − a)
- L{sin at} = a/(s² + a²); L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²)
- L{sinh at} = a/(s² − a²); L{cosh at} = s/(s² − a²)
Linearity: L{af + bg} = aF + bG.

steps.title: Shifting theorems
steps.body:
**First shifting:** L{e^(at)f(t)} = F(s − a).
**Second shifting:** L{f(t − a)u(t − a)} = e^(−as)F(s), where u is the unit step. Also L{u(t − a)} = e^(−as)/s, L{δ(t − a)} = e^(−as).
**Change of scale:** L{f(at)} = (1/a)F(s/a).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L{3t² + 4e^(−2t) − 5 sin 3t} = 6/s³ + 4/(s + 2) − 15/(s² + 9).

**Example 2.** L{e^(2t)cos 3t} = (s − 2)/((s − 2)² + 9).

**Example 3.** f(t) = (t − 1)² for t > 1, 0 otherwise = (t − 1)²u(t − 1) ⇒ L = 2e^(−s)/s³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ (missing +1 in the power).
- First shifting with s + a instead of s − a for e^(at).
- Applying the second shifting theorem without rewriting f in terms of (t − a).

quiz.why: L{tⁿ} = n!/sⁿ⁺¹, so L{t} = 1/s².
L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²). With a = 5: s/(s² + 25).
L{t²} = 2/s³, and by the first shifting theorem the factor eᵗ replaces s with s − 1: 2/(s − 1)³.
By the second shifting theorem, L{u(t − a)} = e^(−as)/s. With a = 2: e^(−2s)/s.
The Laplace transform of the unit impulse δ(t) is 1.

lessons.title: Derivatives, integrals, t·f(t), f(t)/t and periodic functions

scenes.text: A motor driver applies a repeating square wave.
Periodic functions have a neat Laplace formula over one period.

steps.title: Key properties
steps.body:
- L{f′} = sF − f(0); L{f″} = s²F − s f(0) − f′(0)
- L{∫₀ᵗ f du} = F(s)/s
- L{t f(t)} = −F′(s); L{tⁿf} = (−1)ⁿ dⁿF/dsⁿ
- L{f(t)/t} = ∫ₛ^∞ F(u)du (if the limit of f/t at 0 exists)
- Periodic with period T: L{f} = [1/(1 − e^(−sT))]∫₀ᵀ e^(−st)f(t)dt

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L{t sin 2t} = −d/ds[2/(s² + 4)] = 4s/(s² + 4)².

**Example 2.** L{(sin t)/t} = ∫ₛ^∞ du/(u² + 1) = π/2 − tan⁻¹s = cot⁻¹s. Putting s → 0 gives ∫₀^∞ (sin t)/t dt = π/2.

**Example 3.** Square wave f = 1 on (0, a), −1 on (a, 2a), period 2a: ∫₀^(2a)e^(−st)f dt = (1 − e^(−as))²/s ⇒ L = (1/s)tanh(as/2).

steps.title: Evaluating integrals
steps.body: ∫₀^∞ e^(−st)f(t)dt at a given s is just F(s). E.g. ∫₀^∞ t e^(−2t)dt = L{t} at s = 2 = 1/4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign in L{t f} (it is −F′(s)).
- Forgetting initial values in L{f″}.
- Integrating from 0 instead of s to ∞ in the division rule.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀^∞ t e^(−3t) dt using Laplace (decimal)

quiz.why: L{f′(t)} = sF(s) − f(0), by integration by parts.
L{∫₀ᵗ f} = F(s)/s. With f = sin u: [1/(s² + 1)]/s = 1/(s(s² + 1)).
L{(sin t)/t} = tan⁻¹(1/s). At s = 0 this equals π/2, which is ∫₀^∞(sin t)/t dt.
For a periodic function of period T, L{f} = [1/(1 − e^(−sT))]∫₀ᵀ e^(−st)f(t)dt.

scenes.text: After solving in s, Asha has Y(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) and needs y(t).
Partial fractions or convolution bring it back.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- Use the table backwards, with first shifting for (s − a).
- Partial fractions for rational F(s).
- L⁻¹{e^(−as)F(s)} = f(t − a)u(t − a).
- **Convolution:** L⁻¹{F(s)G(s)} = (f * g)(t) = ∫₀ᵗ f(u)g(t − u)du.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) = 1/(s + 1) − 1/(s + 2) ⇒ e^(−t) − e^(−2t).

**Example 2.** (s + 3)/(s² + 4s + 13) = ((s + 2) + 1)/((s + 2)² + 9) ⇒ e^(−2t)(cos 3t + (1/3) sin 3t).

**Example 3 (convolution).** L⁻¹{1/(s(s² + 1))} = ∫₀ᵗ sin u·1 du = 1 − cos t.

**Example 4.** L⁻¹{1/(s² + a²)²} = (sin at − at cos at)/(2a³) by convolving (sin at)/a with itself.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not completing the square before using the shifting theorem.
- Wrong partial-fraction form for repeated factors (need A/(s − a) + B/(s − a)²).
- Forgetting the u(t − a) factor with e^(−as).

quiz.why: Table.
L⁻¹{s/(s² + a²)} = cos at, so with a = 4 it is cos 4t.
1/(s + 2)² is the shift of 1/s² by 2, so the inverse is t e^(−2t).
By the second shifting theorem, L⁻¹{e^(−3s)/s} = u(t − 3), the unit step at t = 3.
The convolution (1 * 1)(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 1·1 du = t.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:

2. Solve for Y(s).

courses.title: Maths II · Unit 4 · Fourier series
courses.summary: Euler's formulas, Dirichlet conditions, even and odd functions, arbitrary period 2L, half-range sine and cosine series, Parseval's identity and harmonic analysis.
outcomes: Compute Fourier coefficients a₀, aₙ, bₙ
Use even/odd symmetry to cut work
Write half-range and arbitrary-period series
Use Parseval's identity and harmonic analysis on data
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A plucked string sounds rich because its shape is a sum of sine waves.
Fourier series find exactly how much of each harmonic is present.

steps.title: Series and coefficients
steps.body:
For f of period 2π: f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx).
a₀ = (1/π)∫₋π^π f dx, aₙ = (1/π)∫₋π^π f cos nx dx, bₙ = (1/π)∫₋π^π f sin nx dx.
**Dirichlet conditions:** f periodic, finitely many discontinuities and extrema in a period, absolutely integrable ⇒ series converges to f where continuous and to the average of the left and right limits at a jump.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** f(x) = x on (−π, π). f is odd ⇒ a₀ = aₙ = 0. bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x sin nx dx = 2(−1)^(n+1)/n.
x = 2(sin x − sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 − …). At x = π/2: π/2 = 2(1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − …) ⇒ π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − … (Gregory series).

**Example 2.** f(x) = x² on (−π, π): even. a₀ = 2π²/3, aₙ = 4(−1)ⁿ/n². x² = π²/3 + 4Σ(−1)ⁿ cos nx/n². At x = π: Σ1/n² = π²/6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ in a₀/2 (some books define a₀ differently — be consistent).
- Sign of (−1)ⁿ from cos nπ.
- Claiming the series equals f at a jump (it gives the mid-value).

activity.text: For an odd function on (−π, π), a₀ = ___ and aₙ = ___.

quiz.why: cos nπ alternates between 1 and −1 as n changes parity, so cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ.

quiz.q: At a jump discontinuity the series converges to
quiz.why: At a jump discontinuity the Fourier series converges to the average of the left and right limits (Dirichlet's theorem).
options: the average of left and right limits

quiz.q: Fourier series of an odd function contains only
quiz.why: For an odd function the cosine coefficients aₙ vanish, so the series has only sine terms.

quiz.q: Using x² series at x = π gives Σ1/n² =
quiz.why: Putting x = π in the Fourier series of x² on (−π, π) gives π² = π²/3 + 4Σ1/n², so Σ1/n² = π²/6.
sin nπ = 0 for every integer n, since sine vanishes at multiples of π.

lessons.title: Arbitrary period, even and odd extensions

scenes.text: Mains voltage repeats every 20 ms, not every 2π.
Scale x → πx/L to use any period 2L.

steps.title: Period 2L
steps.body:
f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙ cos(nπx/L) + bₙ sin(nπx/L)], with aₙ = (1/L)∫₋L^L f cos(nπx/L)dx, bₙ = (1/L)∫₋L^L f sin(nπx/L)dx.
Even f: only cosines, aₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f cos(nπx/L)dx. Odd f: only sines.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** f(x) = |x| on (−1, 1), L = 1, even. a₀ = 2∫₀¹x dx = 1. aₙ = 2∫₀¹ x cos nπx dx = 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(n²π²) ⇒ −4/(n²π²) for odd n.
|x| = ½ − (4/π²)Σ_(odd n) cos(nπx)/n².

**Example 2.** Square wave f = −1 on (−π, 0), 1 on (0, π): odd, bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = 2(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ) ⇒ 4/(nπ) for odd n.
f = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + …).

steps.title: Symmetry shortcuts
steps.body:
- Even × even = even, odd × odd = even, even × odd = odd.
- ∫₋L^L odd = 0; ∫₋L^L even = 2∫₀^L.
- Square wave has only odd harmonics with amplitude ∝ 1/n.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using sin nx instead of sin(nπx/L).
- Applying even/odd shortcuts to functions that are neither.
- Not splitting the integral for piecewise f.

statements.s: The square wave contains only odd harmonics.

quiz.why: For period 2L, the basic functions are cos(nπx/L) and sin(nπx/L).

quiz.q: Square wave amplitude of 3rd harmonic relative to 1st
quiz.why: For a square wave bₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n, so the 3rd harmonic has 1/3 of the amplitude of the first.
x is odd and sin x is odd, and the product of two odd functions is even.

quiz.q: For even f on (−L, L), bₙ =
quiz.why: For an even function f, f(x) sin(nπx/L) is odd, so its integral over (−L, L) is zero, giving bₙ = 0.
a₀ = (1/1)∫₋₁¹|x| dx = 2∫₀¹ x dx = 1.

scenes.text: A rod of length L has its initial temperature given only on (0, L).
We may extend it as odd (sine series) or even (cosine series) depending on boundary conditions.

steps.title: Formulas on (0, L)
steps.body:
**Half-range sine:** f = Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L), bₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f sin(nπx/L)dx (odd extension).
**Half-range cosine:** f = a₀/2 + Σ aₙ cos(nπx/L), aₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f cos(nπx/L)dx (even extension).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sine series of f = 1 on (0, π): bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = 2(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ) ⇒ 1 = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + …).

**Example 2.** Cosine series of f = x on (0, π): a₀ = π, aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x cos nx dx = 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²).
x = π/2 − (4/π)(cos x + cos 3x/9 + cos 5x/25 + …). At x = 0: Σ_(odd) 1/n² = π²/8.

steps.title: Which extension?
steps.body: Ends held at zero (fixed string, rod ends at 0 °C) ⇒ sine series. Insulated ends (zero slope) ⇒ cosine series.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 1/L instead of 2/L in half-range formulas.
- Mixing the extension type with the requested series.
- Losing the a₀/2 term in cosine series.

scenes.text: Power electronics engineers measure total harmonic distortion from sampled current.

steps.title: Parseval's identity
steps.body:
On (−π, π): (1/π)∫₋π^π f² dx = a₀²/2 + Σ(aₙ² + bₙ²).
RMS value: f_rms² = a₀²/4 + ½Σ(aₙ² + bₙ²).

steps.title: Harmonic analysis (tabulated data)
steps.body:
For N equally spaced values over one period:
a₀ = 2·mean(y), aₙ = 2·mean(y cos nx), bₙ = 2·mean(y sin nx).
Amplitude of nth harmonic = √(aₙ² + bₙ²).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor 2 in harmonic-analysis formulas.
- Including the repeated end point (x = 360°) in the data mean.
- Using a₀² instead of a₀²/2 in Parseval.

activity.prompt: Data over one period: y = 1, 3, 5, 3 (4 equal steps). a₀ = 2·mean(y) = ?

quiz.why: Parseval's identity relates the integral of f² to the sum of squares of the Fourier coefficients.
The first harmonic a₁cos x + b₁sin x can be written R sin(x + φ) with amplitude √(a₁² + b₁²).
In numerical harmonic analysis a₀ = (2/N)Σy, which is twice the mean value of y.
Using Parseval's identity with the Fourier series of x gives Σ1/n² = π²/6.

quiz.q: Data points over a period should
quiz.why: In harmonic analysis, data over one period should not repeat the end point (which equals the starting value), so as not to double count it.

questions.why: For an even function bₙ = 0, so the Fourier series has only the constant term and cosine terms.

courses.title: Maths II · Unit 5 · Vector calculus
courses.summary: Gradient, directional derivative and normals, divergence and curl, solenoidal and irrotational fields, line integrals and work, and the theorems of Green, Stokes and Gauss.
outcomes: Compute gradient, divergence, curl and directional derivatives
Identify solenoidal/irrotational fields and scalar potentials
Evaluate line, surface and volume integrals
Apply Green, Stokes and Gauss theorems
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A drone flies over terrain h(x,y). Which way is steepest?
The gradient points uphill fastest; its size is the steepest slope.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
∇ = i∂/∂x + j∂/∂y + k∂/∂z. grad φ = ∇φ.
- Directional derivative along unit vector â: Dₐφ = ∇φ · â.
- Maximum directional derivative = |∇φ|, in the direction of ∇φ.
- ∇φ is normal to the level surface φ = c; unit normal n̂ = ∇φ/|∇φ|.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** φ = x²y + 2xz at (2, −2, 3) along a = 2i − j + 2k.
∇φ = (2xy + 2z)i + x²j + 2xk = (−8 + 6)i + 4j + 4k = −2i + 4j + 4k. â = (2i − j + 2k)/3.
Dₐφ = (−4 − 4 + 8)/3 = 0.

**Example 2.** Unit normal to x² + y² + z² = 9 at (1, 2, 2): ∇ = 2i + 4j + 4k, |∇| = 6 ⇒ n̂ = (i + 2j + 2k)/3.

**Example 3.** Angle between surfaces x² + y² + z² = 9 and z = x² + y² − 3 at (2, −1, 2): n₁ = 4i − 2j + 4k, n₂ = 4i − 2j − k; cos θ = (16 + 4 − 4)/(6√21) = 8/(3√21).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a instead of the unit vector â.
- Evaluating ∇φ symbolically but forgetting to plug in the point.
- Confusing gradient (vector) with directional derivative (scalar).

activity.prompt: φ = x² + y² + z². Max directional derivative at (1, 2, 2) = |∇φ| = ?

quiz.why: The gradient ∇φ is a vector perpendicular (normal) to the level surface φ = c.
options: a vector normal to φ = c

quiz.q: Directional derivative of φ along â
quiz.why: The directional derivative of φ in the direction of the unit vector â is ∇φ · â.
∇(xyz) = (yz, xz, xy). At (1, 1, 1) this is i + j + k.

quiz.q: Max rate of change of φ occurs along
quiz.why: φ changes fastest along ∇φ, since the directional derivative ∇φ·â is largest when â points along ∇φ.
∇r = r/r, the unit vector in the radial direction.

scenes.text: A sprinkler spreads water out — positive divergence.
A whirlpool rotates water — non-zero curl.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For F = F₁i + F₂j + F₃k:
div F = ∇·F = ∂F₁/∂x + ∂F₂/∂y + ∂F₃/∂z (scalar).
curl F = ∇×F = det[[i, j, k],[∂ₓ, ∂ᵧ, ∂_z],[F₁, F₂, F₃]] (vector).
**Solenoidal:** ∇·F = 0. **Irrotational:** ∇×F = 0 ⇒ F = ∇φ (scalar potential).

steps.title: Identities
steps.body:
- curl(grad φ) = 0
- div(curl F) = 0
- ∇·(φF) = φ∇·F + F·∇φ
- ∇²φ = div grad φ (Laplacian)
- ∇·r = 3, ∇×r = 0, ∇²(1/r) = 0 for r ≠ 0

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F = x²yi + yz j + xz²k. ∇·F = 2xy + z + 2xz. ∇×F = (0 − y)i − (z² − 0)j + (0 − x²)k = −yi − z²j − x²k.

**Example 2.** F = (y + z)i + (z + x)j + (x + y)k: ∇×F = (1 − 1)i − (1 − 1)j + (1 − 1)k = 0 ⇒ irrotational. Potential φ = xy + yz + zx.

**Example 3.** Find a so that F = (x + 3y)i + (y − 2z)j + (x + az)k is solenoidal: 1 + 1 + a = 0 ⇒ a = −2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign of the j component of curl (it is −(∂F₃/∂x − ∂F₁/∂z)).
- Treating div as a vector.
- Assuming every solenoidal field is irrotational.

quiz.why: curl r = 0, since the position vector field is irrotational.
curl(grad φ) = 0 is a standard identity (mixed partials are equal).
A field with zero divergence is called solenoidal. Zero curl means irrotational.
Since curl(grad φ) = 0, a gradient field is irrotational.

scenes.text: A robotic arm moves a tool through a force field F along a curve C.
Work = ∫_C F·dr. For conservative fields the path does not matter.

steps.title: Line integral
steps.body:
∫_C F·dr = ∫_C (F₁dx + F₂dy + F₃dz). Parametrise C as r(t), a ≤ t ≤ b: ∫ₐᵇ F(r(t))·r′(t)dt.
If F = ∇φ, ∫_C F·dr = φ(B) − φ(A) (path-independent) and ∮F·dr = 0.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F = x²i + xyj along y = x from (0,0) to (1,1): x = t, y = t: ∫₀¹ (t² + t²)dt = 2/3.

**Example 2.** Same F along y = x²: x = t, y = t², dy = 2t dt: ∫₀¹ (t² + t·t²·2t)dt = 1/3 + 2/5 = 11/15. Different from Example 1 ⇒ F not conservative (check: curl F = yk ≠ 0).

**Example 3.** F = (2xy + z³)i + x²j + 3xz²k is conservative with φ = x²y + xz³. Work from (1, −2, 1) to (3, 1, 4): φ(3,1,4) − φ(1,−2,1) = (9 + 192) − (−2 + 1) = 202.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Forgetting to convert dx, dy into dt.

quiz.q: For a conservative field the line integral depends on

scenes.text: Flux of a fluid out of a closed tank can be found by integrating divergence inside.
Three theorems swap hard integrals for easier ones.

steps.title: The three theorems
steps.body:
**Green (plane):** ∮_C (M dx + N dy) = ∬_R (∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y) dx dy (C anticlockwise).
**Stokes:** ∮_C F·dr = ∬_S (∇×F)·n̂ dS.
**Gauss divergence:** ∯_S F·n̂ dS = ∭_V ∇·F dV.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Green).** ∮(x² − y)dx + x dy around x² + y² = 1: ∂N/∂x − ∂M/∂y = 1 − (−1) = 2 ⇒ 2·π = 2π.

**Example 2 (Gauss).** F = xi + yj + zk over the sphere of radius a: ∇·F = 3 ⇒ flux = 3·(4πa³/3) = 4πa³.

**Example 3 (Gauss on a cube).** F = x²i + y²j + z²k, cube 0 ≤ x, y, z ≤ 1: ∇·F = 2(x + y + z) ⇒ ∭ = 2·(3/2) = 3.

**Example 4 (Stokes).** F = −yi + xj, S = disc of radius 1 in xy-plane: ∇×F = 2k ⇒ ∬2 dS = 2π = ∮F·dr ✔

steps.title: Area by Green
steps.body: Area = ½∮(x dy − y dx). For the ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t: ½∫₀^(2π)ab dt = πab.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clockwise orientation in Green's theorem (gives a minus sign).
- Using Gauss for an open surface.
- Outward vs inward normal.

questions.why: For irrotational F in 2-D we need ∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y = 0. Here ∂(x + 2y)/∂x − ∂(ax + y)/∂y = 1 − 1 = 0 for every a, so it is always irrotational.

questions.why: Take φ = x² + y² − z, so ∇φ = (2x, 2y, −1) = (2, 2, −1) at (1, 1, 2). Its magnitude is 3, so the unit normal is (2i + 2j − k)/3.

Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

questions.why: By Green's theorem, ∮(y dx − x dy) = ∬(∂(−x)/∂x − ∂y/∂y)dA = ∬(−2)dA = −2π for the unit circle.

questions.why: F = ∇(x² + y²), so the work is φ(1, 2) − φ(0, 0) = 1 + 4 − 0 = 5.

questions.why: By Gauss's theorem, flux = ∭(3x² + 3y² + 3z²)dV = 3∭r²dV = 3 × 4π/5 = 12π/5.

questions.why: ∇·v = ∂(x − 2y)/∂x + ∂(y + z)/∂y + ∂(az − x)/∂z = 1 + 1 + a. For zero we need a = −2.

questions.why: F = yi + xj = ∇(xy), so the line integral depends only on the end points: 2 × 3 − 0 = 6.

questions.why: ∇²(1/r) = 0 for r ≠ 0, because 1/r is a harmonic function (the Newtonian potential).

questions.why: div F = 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. By Gauss's theorem flux = 9 × volume = 9 × 8 = 72.

scenes.text: Aerodynamicists describe 2-D airflow with a single complex function w = φ + iψ.
It only works if w is analytic — and the test is the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: f(z) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y), z = x + iy. f is differentiable at z₀ if lim [f(z₀ + Δz) − f(z₀)]/Δz exists independent of the direction of Δz → 0. **Analytic** in a region if differentiable at every point of it.

steps.title: Cauchy–Riemann equations
steps.body:
Cartesian: uₓ = v_y, u_y = −vₓ. Then f′(z) = uₓ + ivₓ.
Polar: u_r = (1/r)v_θ, v_r = −(1/r)u_θ.
CR equations are necessary; with continuous partials they are also sufficient.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** f = z² = (x² − y²) + i(2xy): uₓ = 2x = v_y, u_y = −2y = −vₓ ✔ analytic everywhere; f′ = 2x + 2iy = 2z.

**Example 2.** f = z̄ = x − iy: uₓ = 1, v_y = −1 ✘ — nowhere analytic.

**Example 3.** f = |z|² = x² + y²: u = x² + y², v = 0. CR: 2x = 0 and 2y = 0 hold only at z = 0 ⇒ differentiable only at the origin, analytic nowhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign in u_y = −vₓ.
- Calling a function analytic because CR holds at a single point.
- Forgetting continuity of partials when using CR as a sufficient test.

statements.why: u = eˣcos y, v = eˣsin y satisfy CR.

quiz.why: The Cauchy–Riemann equations for f = u + iv are u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x.
For an analytic function f′(z) = u_x + i v_x, found by differentiating along the real direction.
sin z is analytic everywhere (entire). |z| and z̄ fail the CR equations, and 1/z has a singularity at 0.
z² = (x + iy)² = x² − y² + 2ixy, so the imaginary part v = 2xy.
In polar form the Cauchy–Riemann equations are u_r = (1/r)v_θ and v_r = −(1/r)u_θ.

scenes.text: Steady temperature in a thin plate satisfies Laplace's equation.
The real and imaginary parts of analytic functions are exactly such harmonic functions — and their level curves cross at right angles.

steps.title: Harmonic functions
steps.body: u is harmonic if uₓₓ + u_yy = 0. Real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic; v is the **harmonic conjugate** of u. The families u = c₁ and v = c₂ are orthogonal.

steps.title: Finding v and f
steps.body:
**Via CR:** dv = vₓdx + v_ydy = −u_y dx + uₓ dy; integrate (exact differential).
**Milne-Thomson:** f′(z) = uₓ(z, 0) − iu_y(z, 0). Integrate in z: f(z) = ∫[uₓ(z,0) − iu_y(z,0)]dz + C.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x² − y² + x. Harmonic: 2 − 2 = 0 ✔. uₓ = 2x + 1, u_y = −2y.
Milne-Thomson: f′ = (2z + 1) − i(0) ⇒ f = z² + z + C. So v = 2xy + y.

**Example 2.** u = eˣ cos y: uₓ = eˣ cos y, u_y = −eˣ sin y. f′ = e^z − i·0 ⇒ f = e^z + C, v = eˣ sin y.

**Example 3.** Given v = 2xy (imaginary part), use f′ = v_y(z,0) + ivₓ(z,0) = 2z + 0 ⇒ f = z² + C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting x = z, y = 0 before differentiating (differentiate first).
- Missing the minus sign in uₓ − iu_y.
- Not checking that u is harmonic first.

u = x is the real part of f(z) = z, so the harmonic conjugate is v = y.

scenes.text: Electrostatics in an awkward region can be mapped to a simple strip or half-plane.
Analytic maps preserve angles — that is what 'conformal' means.

steps.title: Conformal maps
steps.body:
w = f(z) is conformal at z₀ if f is analytic and f′(z₀) ≠ 0: angles (magnitude and sense) between curves are preserved.
- w = z + c: translation
- w = az: rotation by arg a and magnification |a|
- w = 1/z: inversion + reflection
- w = z²: doubles angles at origin (not conformal at 0)

steps.title: Bilinear (Möbius) transformation
steps.body:
w = (az + b)/(cz + d), ad − bc ≠ 0. Maps circles/lines to circles/lines. Determined uniquely by three point images, using the cross-ratio:
(w − w₁)(w₂ − w₃)/[(w − w₃)(w₂ − w₁)] = (z − z₁)(z₂ − z₃)/[(z − z₃)(z₂ − z₁)].
Fixed points: solve z = (az + b)/(cz + d).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Fixed points of w = (z − 1)/(z + 1): z² + z = z − 1 ⇒ z² = −1 ⇒ z = ±i.

**Example 2.** Image of |z| = 2 under w = 1/z: |w| = 1/2 (circle radius ½).

**Example 3.** Bilinear map sending z = 0, 1, ∞ to w = −1, 0, 1: try w = (z − 1)/(z + 1): z = 0 → −1 ✔, z = 1 → 0 ✔, z → ∞ → 1 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling w = z² conformal at z = 0 (f′(0) = 0).
- Forgetting the condition ad − bc ≠ 0.
- Arithmetic slips in the cross-ratio order.

quiz.why: A mapping is conformal (angle preserving) where f is analytic and f′(z) ≠ 0.
Under w = 1/z, |w| = 1/|z|. So |z| = 3 maps to the circle |w| = 1/3.
Fixed points satisfy z = (z − 1)/(z + 1), so z² + z = z − 1, i.e. z² = −1 and z = ±i.

quiz.q: A bilinear map is fixed by images of
quiz.why: A bilinear transformation has three free parameters, so it is determined by the images of three distinct points (cross-ratio).

quiz.q: w = z² is NOT conformal at
quiz.why: w = z² has f′(z) = 2z, which is 0 at z = 0, so the mapping is not conformal there.

Understanding e^z, log z and powers in the complex plane makes phasors natural.

steps.title: Exponential, trig and log
steps.body:
- e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y); periodic with period 2πi.
- sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i), cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2; |sin z| can exceed 1.
- log z = ln|z| + i(arg z + 2nπ); principal value Log z uses −π < arg z ≤ π.
- z^c = e^(c log z).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** e^(iπ) = −1 (Euler's identity).

**Example 2.** Log(−1) = ln 1 + iπ = iπ.

**Example 3.** iⁱ = e^(i log i) = e^(i·iπ/2) = e^(−π/2) ≈ 0.208 (principal value — a real number!).

**Example 4.** Solve cos z = 2: e^(iz) + e^(−iz) = 4 ⇒ e^(iz) = 2 ± √3 ⇒ z = 2nπ − i ln(2 ± √3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming |sin z| ≤ 1 for complex z.
- Treating log z as single-valued.
- Forgetting the 2nπ in general solutions.

iⁱ = e^(i log i) = e^(i · iπ/2) = e^(−π/2), a real number.
The principal logarithm of −1 is ln|−1| + i Arg(−1) = 0 + iπ = iπ.
Yes: for z = iy, cos(iy) = cosh y, which can be larger than 1. Real cosine is bounded by 1, but complex cosine is not.

questions.q: Which is not analytic anywhere?
questions.why: f(z) = z̄ = x − iy has u_x = 1 but v_y = −1, so the CR equations fail everywhere. It is nowhere analytic.

questions.why: A harmonic function satisfies Laplace's equation, u_xx + u_yy = 0.

questions.q: Real part of e^z
questions.why: e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y), so the real part is eˣ cos y.

questions.why: (x + iy)² = x² − y² + 2ixy, so the expression is z².

questions.why: By Milne-Thomson, f(z) = 2z + iz², which gives v = 2y + x² − y² (up to a constant).
