courses.title: Engineering Physics · Unit 5 · Electromagnetic theory
courses.summary: Gauss's law and its applications, Faraday's law, Ampère's law and displacement current, Maxwell's equations in integral and differential form, electromagnetic waves in free space, and energy flow with the Poynting vector.
outcomes: Apply Gauss's law to symmetric charge distributions
Explain displacement current and complete Ampère's law
Write Maxwell's equations and derive the wave equation
Compute wave speed, impedance, intensity and Poynting vector
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Coaxial cables carry TV signals with a metal sheath around the inner wire.
Gauss's law explains why the field outside a closed conductor can be zero.

steps.title: Gauss's law
steps.body: Integral: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Differential: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀. Choose a Gaussian surface where E is constant and normal (or parallel) to the surface.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (line charge λ).** Cylinder radius r: E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ ⇒ E = λ/(2πε₀r).

**Example 2 (infinite sheet σ).** Pillbox: 2EA = σA/ε₀ ⇒ E = σ/(2ε₀). For a conductor surface E = σ/ε₀.

**Example 3 (uniform sphere R, charge Q).** Outside: E = Q/(4πε₀r²). Inside: E = Qr/(4πε₀R³) (rises linearly).

steps.title: Potential and related results
steps.body: E = −∇V. Poisson's equation ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀; Laplace's ∇²V = 0 in charge-free space. Inside a conductor E = 0 and V is constant; excess charge resides on the surface.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Gauss's law to find E for shapes without symmetry (true but useless).
- Using the total charge instead of the enclosed charge inside a sphere.
- Forgetting the factor 2 for a non-conducting sheet.

quiz.why: Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enclosed/ε₀.
Gauss's law in differential form is ∇·E = ρ/ε₀.

quiz.q: Field inside a uniformly charged solid sphere at r < R
quiz.why: Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, Q_enclosed ∝ r³ and the area ∝ r², so E ∝ r.
Laplace's equation ∇²V = 0 applies in regions with no free charge (ρ = 0). With charge, Poisson's equation applies.

quiz.q: Excess charge on a conductor resides
quiz.why: Excess charge on a conductor resides on its surface, since the field inside must be zero in equilibrium.

lessons.title: Faraday's law, Ampère's law and displacement current

scenes.text: While a capacitor charges, current flows in the wires but no charge crosses the gap.
Yet a magnetic field surrounds the gap — Maxwell's displacement current explains it.

steps.title: Faraday and Ampère
steps.body:
Faraday: ∮E·dl = −dΦ_B/dt ⇔ ∇×E = −∂B/∂t (Lenz's law gives the sign).
Ampère (static): ∮B·dl = μ₀I ⇔ ∇×B = μ₀J. Taking divergence gives ∇·J = 0 — contradicts the continuity equation ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t for time-varying fields.

steps.title: Displacement current
steps.body: Maxwell added J_d = ε₀∂E/∂t: ∇×B = μ₀(J + ε₀∂E/∂t). In a capacitor gap, I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = C dV/dt equals the conduction current in the wires.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 2 µF capacitor with dV/dt = 10⁶ V/s: I_d = 2 A.

**Example 2.** Loop of area 0.1 m² in B changing at 0.5 T/s: emf = 0.05 V.

**Example 3.** Circular plates radius R, I_d = I: B at r < R in the gap = μ₀Ir/(2πR²); at r = R, B = μ₀I/(2πR).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking displacement current is a flow of charge.
- Forgetting the minus sign (Lenz) in Faraday's law.
- Using total I_d instead of the enclosed part for r < R.

activity.prompt: Capacitor C = 5 µF, dV/dt = 2×10⁵ V/s. Displacement current (A)?

quiz.why: The displacement current density is J_d = ε₀ ∂E/∂t.
Faraday's law in differential form is ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t.

quiz.q: Displacement current was introduced to satisfy
quiz.why: Maxwell added the displacement current so that Ampère's law is consistent with the continuity equation (charge conservation).

quiz.q: In the capacitor gap, I_d equals
quiz.why: Between the plates of a charging capacitor the displacement current equals the conduction current in the wires, which keeps the current continuous.

quiz.q: emf from Φ_B changing at 3 Wb/s
quiz.why: By Faraday's law |emf| = |dΦ/dt| = 3 V.

scenes.text: Radio, Wi-Fi, light and X-rays are all one phenomenon.
Maxwell's equations predict waves travelling at 1/√(μ₀ε₀) — the speed of light.

steps.title: The four equations (differential form)
steps.body:
∇·D = ρ (Gauss)
∇·B = 0 (no magnetic monopoles)
∇×E = −∂B/∂t (Faraday)
∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t (Ampère–Maxwell)
with D = εE, B = μH, J = σE.

steps.title: Wave equation in free space
steps.body:
With ρ = 0, J = 0: ∇×(∇×E) = −μ₀ε₀∂²E/∂t² and ∇×∇×E = ∇(∇·E) − ∇²E = −∇²E ⇒ ∇²E = μ₀ε₀∂²E/∂t². Same for B. Speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s.
Plane wave: E, B and propagation direction mutually perpendicular (transverse); E₀/B₀ = c; intrinsic impedance η₀ = √(μ₀/ε₀) ≈ 377 Ω.
In a medium: v = 1/√(με) = c/n.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** c = 1/√(4π×10⁻⁷ × 8.854×10⁻¹²) = 2.998×10⁸ m/s.

**Example 2.** E₀ = 30 V/m in free space: B₀ = 30/3×10⁸ = 10⁻⁷ T; H₀ = E₀/377 = 0.0796 A/m.

**Example 3.** Wave in glass with εᵣ = 2.25 (μᵣ = 1): v = c/1.5 = 2×10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the vector identity in deriving the wave equation.
- Writing E₀/B₀ = η₀ (it is E₀/H₀ = η₀; E₀/B₀ = c).
- Mixing D with E inside materials.

items: Take the curl of both sides

quiz.why: ∇·B = 0 means that magnetic field lines have no sources or sinks, i.e. there are no magnetic monopoles.

quiz.q: Speed of EM waves in vacuum
quiz.why: The speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).
The impedance of free space is η₀ = √(μ₀/ε₀) ≈ 377 Ω (120π).
EM waves are transverse: E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
In a plane EM wave in vacuum, E₀/B₀ = c.

lessons.title: Energy flow and the Poynting vector

scenes.text: Sunlight delivers about 1.36 kW per square metre above the atmosphere.
That energy flow per unit area is the Poynting vector.

steps.title: Poynting theorem
steps.body: S = E × H (W/m²) gives the direction and rate of energy flow. Energy density u = ½ε₀E² + ½B²/μ₀ (equal electric and magnetic shares in a plane wave). Time-averaged intensity I = ⟨S⟩ = E₀²/(2η₀) = ½cε₀E₀². Radiation pressure = I/c (absorbing surface), 2I/c (perfect reflector).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Solar intensity 1360 W/m²: E₀ = √(2Iη₀) = √(2 × 1360 × 377) ≈ 1013 V/m; B₀ = 3.4 µT.

**Example 2.** A 100 W bulb radiating uniformly: at 2 m, I = 100/(4π·4) ≈ 2 W/m² ⇒ E_rms = √(Iη₀) ≈ 27 V/m.

**Example 3.** Radiation pressure of sunlight on an absorbing sail: 1360/3×10⁸ ≈ 4.5 µPa.

steps.title: Engineering link
steps.body: Antenna design, microwave heating, solar sails, EMI safety limits and fibre power budgets all rely on S and intensity calculations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the ½ for time averages of sinusoidal fields.
- Using peak instead of RMS values inconsistently.
- Pointing S along E instead of E × H.

activity.prompt: Plane wave with E₀ = 377 V/m in vacuum. Average intensity E₀²/(2·377) in W/m²?

quiz.why: The Poynting vector is S = E × H, giving the energy flow per unit area per unit time.

quiz.q: Average intensity of a plane wave
quiz.why: The time-averaged intensity of a plane wave is I = E₀²/(2η₀).

quiz.q: Radiation pressure on a perfect reflector
quiz.why: A perfect reflector reverses the photon momentum, so the radiation pressure is 2I/c (compared with I/c for a perfect absorber).

quiz.q: Electric and magnetic energy densities in a plane wave are
quiz.why: In a plane EM wave the electric and magnetic energy densities are equal.
S = E × H points along the direction of wave propagation.

questions.q: Gauss's law relates flux to
questions.why: Gauss's law relates the electric flux through a closed surface to the enclosed charge.

questions.q: Maxwell's equation with no sources term
questions.why: ∇·B = 0 is the Maxwell equation with no source term, as there are no magnetic monopoles.

questions.q: c in vacuum ≈
questions.why: The speed of light in vacuum is c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.q: Field near an infinite sheet σ
questions.why: Using a Gaussian pillbox, the field near an infinite sheet is σ/(2ε₀), since flux leaves through both faces.

questions.q: Displacement current exists in
questions.why: Displacement current exists where the electric field changes with time, such as in the gap of a charging capacitor.
options: a DC resistor in steady state

Assertion (A): A time-varying electric field produces a magnetic field.  Reason (R): The Ampère–Maxwell law includes ∂D/∂t.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: the Ampère–Maxwell law contains ∂D/∂t, which says a changing electric field acts like a current and produces a magnetic field.

questions.why: For a line charge E = 2kλ/r = 2 × 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/0.1 = 180 V/m.

E_rms at 1 m from a 10 W isotropic source

questions.why: At the plate edge B = μ₀I_d/(2πR) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 2/0.05 = 8 × 10⁻⁶ T = 8 μT.

questions.why: E ∝ r inside a uniformly charged sphere, so at r = R/2 it is half of the surface value.

questions.why: For an absorber, force = IA/c = 1360 × 10/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ N = 45 μN.

questions.q: Continuity equation
questions.why: The continuity equation expresses charge conservation: ∇·J + ∂ρ/∂t = 0.

questions.q: Energy density of a field E = 3×10⁴ V/m (electric part, ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹²)
questions.why: The electric energy density is u = ½ε₀E² = 0.5 × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × (3 × 10⁴)² ≈ 4 × 10⁻³ J/m³.

questions.why: The Compton shift is maximum at φ = 180°: 2 × 2.43 = 4.86 pm.

questions.q: Polarisers at 30°: transmitted fraction of polarised light
questions.why: By Malus' law the fraction is cos²30° = (0.866)² = 0.75.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Single-mode fibres have no intermodal dispersion.  Reason (R): Only one guided mode propagates.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: with only one guided mode there is no spread in arrival times between modes, so there is no intermodal dispersion.

questions.q: Electron confined to 1 nm box: E₁ ≈
questions.why: For an electron in a 1 nm box, E₁ = h²/(8mL²) ≈ 0.38 eV.

questions.q: Bragg reflection λ = 1.5 Å, θ = 30°, n = 1 ⇒ d =
Intrinsic carrier density depends strongly on
questions.why: The intrinsic carrier density depends exponentially on temperature and band gap, nᵢ ∝ T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT).

questions.q: Newton's rings: D₁₀² − D₅² = 0.12 cm², R = 100 cm. λ =
questions.why: Dₙ² = 4nλR, so D₁₀² − D₅² = 4 × 5 × λR. 0.12 = 20 × 100 × λ gives λ = 6 × 10⁻⁵ cm = 600 nm.

questions.q: V-number for a = 25 µm, NA = 0.2, λ = 0.85 µm
questions.why: V = 2πa NA/λ = 2π × 25 × 0.2/0.85 ≈ 37. This is far above 2.405, so the fibre is multimode.

questions.q: Uncertainty in velocity of an electron with Δx = 1 nm
Case: Solar panel receives 1000 W/m². E₀ of the light ≈
Minimum thickness of soap film (μ = 1.33) appearing dark in reflection for 600 nm (non-zero)
questions.why: A film that appears dark by reflection has 2μt = nλ. The thinnest non-zero thickness is t = λ/2μ = 600/(2 × 1.33) ≈ 226 nm.

questions.q: Resolving sodium doublet (Δλ = 0.6 nm) with a 1000-line grating requires order
questions.why: The doublet needs R = λ/Δλ ≈ 982 = nN. With N = 1000 lines, the first order (n = 1) just does it.

questions.q: Hall: R_H = 3.66×10⁻⁴ m³/C, σ = 112 S/m ⇒ mobility
questions.why: Mobility μ = σR_H = 112 × 3.66 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 0.041 m²/V·s.

uni-common-sciences-b.description: First-year Engineering Chemistry, unit by unit: water technology, electrochemistry and corrosion, polymers, fuels and spectroscopy — with solved numericals, quizzes and unit exams.

courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 1 · Water technology
courses.summary: Hardness of water and its estimation by EDTA, alkalinity, boiler troubles, softening by lime–soda, zeolite and ion exchange, and drinking-water treatment including reverse osmosis and disinfection.
outcomes: Classify and calculate hardness in CaCO₃ equivalents
Estimate hardness by EDTA titration
Explain scale, sludge, priming, foaming and caustic embrittlement
Compare softening methods and compute lime–soda requirements
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Hardness of water and its units

scenes.text: In a hostel with borewell water, soap forms a curdy scum instead of lather.
Calcium and magnesium salts — hardness — are to blame.

steps.title: Types of hardness
steps.body:
- **Temporary (carbonate):** Ca(HCO₃)₂, Mg(HCO₃)₂ — removed by boiling: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂.
- **Permanent (non-carbonate):** chlorides and sulphates of Ca, Mg — not removed by boiling.
Hardness is expressed as **CaCO₃ equivalent** = (mass of salt × 100)/(molar mass of salt) for divalent salts (equivalent weight ratio 50/eq. wt).

steps.title: Units
steps.body:
1 ppm = 1 mg/L = 1 part CaCO₃ per 10⁶ parts water.
1 °Clarke = 1 grain/gallon (imperial) = 14.3 ppm; 1 °French = 10 ppm.
Multiplication factors (to CaCO₃): Ca(HCO₃)₂ 100/162, Mg(HCO₃)₂ 100/146, CaSO₄ 100/136, CaCl₂ 100/111, MgSO₄ 100/120, MgCl₂ 100/95.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Water contains Ca(HCO₃)₂ 16.2 mg/L, MgCl₂ 9.5 mg/L, CaSO₄ 13.6 mg/L.
Temporary = 16.2 × 100/162 = 10 ppm. Permanent = 9.5 × 100/95 + 13.6 × 100/136 = 10 + 10 = 20 ppm. Total = 30 ppm.

**Example 2.** 30 ppm in °Clarke = 30/14.3 ≈ 2.1 °Cl; in °Fr = 3 °Fr.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting NaCl or KCl as hardness (only Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ and some heavy metals).
- Using molar mass 100 for MgCO₃ (it is 84).
- Mixing mg/L and g/L.

quiz.q: Hardness is expressed in terms of
quiz.why: Hardness of water is expressed as the equivalent amount of CaCO₃ (in ppm or mg/L), as a common standard.
1 ppm = 1 mg per litre, since a litre of dilute water weighs 1 kg = 10⁶ mg.
Boiling removes temporary hardness, since the bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium decompose to insoluble carbonates.
CaCO₃ equivalent = mass × 100/molar mass = 27.2 × 100/136 = 20 ppm.
1 °Clarke is 1 grain of CaCO₃ per gallon (70,000 parts), which is about 14.3 ppm.

story.title: Lab test at a water plant

scenes.text: A chemist titrates 50 mL of tap water with EDTA using Eriochrome Black T.
Wine-red turns blue at the end point — hardness is calculated in minutes.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
EDTA (disodium salt) forms stable 1:1 complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ at pH ≈ 10 (NH₄Cl–NH₄OH buffer). Indicator EBT forms a weak wine-red complex with metal ions; when EDTA removes all metal, free EBT shows **blue**.
Steps: standardise EDTA with standard hard water (1 mg CaCO₃/mL) → titrate sample (total hardness) → boil, filter, titrate (permanent hardness) → temporary = total − permanent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 50 mL standard hard water (1 mg CaCO₃/mL) needs 20 mL EDTA ⇒ 1 mL EDTA ≡ 2.5 mg CaCO₃.
50 mL sample needs 15 mL ⇒ total hardness = 15 × 2.5 × 1000/50 = 750 ppm.
After boiling, 50 mL needs 10 mL ⇒ permanent = 500 ppm; temporary = 250 ppm.

**Example 2.** 0.01 M EDTA, 100 mL sample consumes 12 mL: moles = 1.2×10⁻⁴ ⇒ CaCO₃ = 12 mg ⇒ 120 ppm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running the titration without the pH 10 buffer.
- Forgetting to scale to 1000 mL for ppm.
- Reporting temporary hardness without the boiled-sample titration.

activity.prompt: 0.01 M EDTA: 50 mL water uses 8 mL. Hardness in ppm (1 mol CaCO₃ = 100 g)?

quiz.q: EDTA titration is done at pH
quiz.why: The EDTA titration is carried out at pH about 10, using an ammonia buffer.

quiz.q: Colour at the end point with EBT
quiz.why: EBT is wine-red when bound to metal ions and turns blue at the end point, once EDTA has taken the metal and frees the indicator.
EDTA is hexadentate and forms a 1:1 complex with metal ions.
For permanent hardness the water is boiled and filtered first, to remove temporary hardness, and then the remaining hardness is titrated.
Temporary hardness = total hardness − permanent hardness.

scenes.text: A textile mill's boiler shows a thick white scale on its tubes.
Scale insulates the tubes, wastes fuel and can cause overheating and failure.

steps.title: Problems from hard water
steps.body:
- **Sludge:** soft loose deposits (MgCO₃, MgCl₂, CaCl₂) in cooler parts — removed by blow-down.
- **Scale:** hard adherent deposits — CaSO₄ (solubility falls with temperature), CaCO₃ (at high pressure, from Ca(HCO₃)₂), Mg(OH)₂ (from MgCl₂ hydrolysis), CaSiO₃.
- **Priming:** water droplets carried with steam (wet steam) — high velocity, sudden boiling, faulty design.
- **Foaming:** stable bubbles due to oils/alkali — fix with antifoam (castor oil in small amounts) or removing oil.
- **Caustic embrittlement:** NaOH concentrating in hair-line cracks at high pressure attacks stressed steel — prevent with sodium phosphate (instead of Na₂CO₃), tannin or lignin.
- **Boiler corrosion:** dissolved O₂ (remove with hydrazine N₂H₄ or Na₂SO₃), CO₂, acids from MgCl₂ hydrolysis.

steps.title: Internal treatment (conditioning)
steps.body: Colloidal conditioning (tannin, agar) for low-pressure boilers; phosphate conditioning (Na₃PO₄ for acidic water, Na₂HPO₄ for weakly alkaline water, NaH₂PO₄ for too-alkaline water) forms soft calcium phosphate sludge; carbonate conditioning; calgon (sodium hexametaphosphate) forms soluble complex with Ca²⁺.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Why is CaSO₄ scale dangerous? Its solubility decreases as temperature rises, so it deposits hard on hot tube surfaces.

**Example 2.** O₂ removal: N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O (no salts added). 2Na₂SO₃ + O₂ → 2Na₂SO₄ (adds sulphate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing sludge (loose) with scale (adherent).
- Using excess Na₂SO₃ at high pressure — it can produce SO₂.
- Thinking priming and foaming are the same.

activity.prompt: Match the boiler problem with a remedy

quiz.why: A hard, adherent deposit on boiler walls is called scale.
Caustic embrittlement is cracking of boiler metal caused by NaOH concentrating in cracks and rivet joints.
Hydrazine (N₂H₄) removes dissolved oxygen: N₂H₄ + O₂ → N₂ + 2H₂O, without leaving solids.
Calgon is sodium hexametaphosphate, used in conditioning to keep calcium in solution as a soluble complex.
Priming is the carry-over of water droplets with the steam from the boiler.

scenes.text: A municipal plant must supply safe water to a million people.
Industries need softer water still — lime–soda, zeolite or ion exchange.

steps.title: Softening processes
steps.body:
- **Lime–soda:** lime Ca(OH)₂ removes temporary hardness, Mg salts, CO₂, HCO₃⁻; soda Na₂CO₃ removes Ca permanent hardness. Cold process (coagulant needed) vs hot (faster, ~15–30 ppm residual).
- **Zeolite (permutit):** Na₂Ze + Ca²⁺ → CaZe + 2Na⁺; regenerate with brine. Residual ~10 ppm; not for acidic or turbid water.
- **Ion exchange (demineralisation):** cation resin (RH) then anion resin (ROH) — water ~0–2 ppm; regenerate with acid and alkali.
- **Reverse osmosis:** pressure > osmotic pressure through semipermeable membrane; desalination of sea/brackish water.

steps.title: Lime–soda requirement (per litre, in CaCO₃ equivalents)
steps.body:
Lime = (74/100)[Temp Ca + 2 Temp Mg + Perm (Mg + Fe + Al) + CO₂ + H⁺ (HCl/H₂SO₄) + HCO₃⁻ − NaAlO₂ ] mg/L.
Soda = (106/100)[Perm (Ca + Mg + Fe + Al) + H⁺ − HCO₃⁻] mg/L.
Multiply by volume and add % purity correction.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Water: Ca(HCO₃)₂ = 162 ppm, MgSO₄ = 120 ppm (as salts). CaCO₃ eq: 100 and 100.
Lime = 0.74(100 + 100) = 148 mg/L; soda = 1.06(100) = 106 mg/L. For 10⁶ L: 148 kg lime, 106 kg soda (pure).

**Example 2.** Drinking water: sedimentation → coagulation (alum) → filtration → disinfection by chlorine (HOCl), break-point chlorination, ozone or UV. Break-point = dose where residual free chlorine starts rising after destroying ammonia/organics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that Mg temporary hardness needs 2 equivalents of lime.
- Adding soda for MgSO₄ only (Mg permanent needs both lime and soda).
- Ignoring purity (e.g. 90% lime ⇒ divide by 0.9).

quiz.why: The zeolite process leaves a residual hardness of about 10 ppm.
Demineralised water is made using a cation exchange resin (H⁺ form) and an anion exchange resin (OH⁻ form) in sequence.
In reverse osmosis, a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the salt side, which forces water across the membrane.
Soda (Na₂CO₃) removes permanent calcium hardness by precipitating CaCO₃: Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃ + 2NaCl.
Break-point chlorination ensures a free residual chlorine, after all chlorine-demanding substances are oxidised.

questions.q: Unit of hardness
questions.why: Hardness is reported in ppm (mg/L) as CaCO₃.

questions.q: EBT gives what colour with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺
questions.why: EBT forms a wine-red complex with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺. At the end point it turns blue.

questions.q: Which causes permanent hardness?
questions.why: CaSO₄ is a non-carbonate (sulphate) salt that stays in water on boiling, so it causes permanent hardness. The bicarbonates cause temporary hardness.

questions.q: CaCO₃ eq of 9.5 ppm MgCl₂
questions.why: CaCO₃ equivalent = mass × 100/molar mass of salt = 9.5 × 100/95 = 10 ppm (MgCl₂ = 95 g/mol).

questions.q: Zeolite is regenerated with
questions.why: An exhausted zeolite (calcium or magnesium form) is regenerated by washing with concentrated brine (NaCl), which restores the sodium form.

questions.q: Scale due to decreasing solubility on heating
questions.why: CaSO₄ has an inverse solubility: it becomes less soluble as temperature rises, so it deposits as hard scale in boilers.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ion-exchange water is suitable for high-pressure boilers.  Reason (R): It removes nearly all ions, including hardness.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: ion-exchange (demineralised) water has almost no dissolved ions, including hardness salts and silica, so it does not form scale or deposits at high pressure and temperature.

questions.q: EDTA: 1 mL ≡ 1 mg CaCO₃; 100 mL sample takes 25 mL. Hardness
questions.why: 1 mL EDTA ≡ 1 mg CaCO₃, so 25 mL means 25 mg CaCO₃ in 100 mL. Per litre that is 250 mg/L = 250 ppm.

questions.q: Lime required for 100 ppm temporary Mg hardness (as CaCO₃) per litre
questions.why: Mg(HCO₃)₂ hardness needs 2 equivalents of Ca(OH)₂. Lime = 0.74 × 2 × 100 = 148 mg per litre (the 0.74 converts CaCO₃ equivalent to Ca(OH)₂).

questions.q: Phosphate conditioning for acidic boiler water uses
questions.why: Acidic water needs the alkaline trisodium phosphate; NaH₂PO₄ suits too-alkaline water.

questions.q: Case: Water has Ca(HCO₃)₂ 32.4 ppm, Mg(HCO₃)₂ 29.2 ppm, CaSO₄ 13.6 ppm. Total hardness
For that water, temporary hardness
questions.why: Temporary hardness comes from the bicarbonates: 20 + 20 = 40 ppm (CaSO₄ gives permanent hardness).

questions.q: Lime for that water per litre (as Ca(OH)₂)
questions.why: Lime = 0.74[temporary Ca + 2 × temporary Mg] = 0.74(20 + 2 × 20) = 0.74 × 60 = 44.4 mg per litre.

questions.q: Soda for that water per litre
questions.why: Soda removes permanent hardness: 1.06 × 10 = 10.6 mg per litre (from CaSO₄, 10 ppm as CaCO₃).

questions.q: RO membranes are commonly made of
questions.why: Reverse osmosis membranes are made of cellulose acetate or polyamide (thin-film composite polymers).

courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 2 · Electrochemistry, batteries and corrosion
courses.summary: Electrode potentials and the Nernst equation, reference electrodes, galvanic cells, batteries (lead–acid, Li-ion) and fuel cells, mechanisms of dry and wet corrosion, factors affecting corrosion and protection methods.
outcomes: Calculate cell EMF with the Nernst equation
Describe primary, secondary batteries and fuel cells
Explain dry, wet, galvanic and differential-aeration corrosion
Choose corrosion-control methods for real cases
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Electrode potential, Nernst equation and cells

scenes.text: Zinc and copper strips in a lemon light a small LED.
The EMF comes from the difference in electrode potentials.

steps.title: Cells and potentials
steps.body:
Galvanic cell: anode (oxidation, −), cathode (reduction, +). E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode (reduction potentials). ΔG° = −nFE°; spontaneous if E > 0.
Reference electrodes: SHE (0 V), calomel (SCE, 0.242 V saturated), Ag/AgCl. Glass electrode measures pH.

steps.title: Nernst equation
steps.body:
For aA + ne⁻ → products: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q at 298 K.
Cell: E = E° − (0.0591/n) log([products]/[reactants]). At equilibrium E = 0 ⇒ log K = nE°/0.0591.
Concentration cell: E = (0.0591/n) log(C₂/C₁).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Daniell cell Zn|Zn²⁺(0.1 M)||Cu²⁺(1 M)|Cu, E° = 1.10 V: E = 1.10 − (0.0591/2) log(0.1/1) = 1.10 + 0.0296 = 1.13 V.

**Example 2.** ΔG° for Daniell: −2 × 96500 × 1.10 = −212 kJ.

**Example 3.** Concentration cell Cu|Cu²⁺(0.01 M)||Cu²⁺(0.1 M)|Cu: E = (0.0591/2)log 10 = 0.0296 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting oxidation potentials incorrectly (use reduction potentials, cathode − anode).
- Multiplying E° when balancing equations (E° is intensive — do not multiply).
- Using ln with 0.0591 (0.0591 already includes the conversion to log₁₀).

quiz.q: Anode in a galvanic cell is
quiz.why: In a galvanic cell the anode is where oxidation occurs, and electrons leave from it, so it is the negative terminal.
ΔG° = −nFE°. A positive E° gives a negative ΔG° (spontaneous).
The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference and is defined as 0 V.
At 298 K the Nernst equation is E = E° − (0.0591/n) log Q, so the factor is 0.0591/n.
A spontaneous cell reaction has a positive EMF (E > 0), which corresponds to ΔG < 0.

scenes.text: An e-scooter runs on a lithium-ion pack; an inverter backup uses lead–acid.
Different chemistries trade energy density, cost and safety.

steps.title: Common batteries
steps.body:
- **Primary (non-rechargeable):** dry cell (Zn | NH₄Cl, MnO₂ | C), ~1.5 V; alkaline cell.
- **Lead–acid (secondary):** Pb | H₂SO₄ | PbO₂. Discharge: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O; ~2 V per cell; acid density falls on discharge.
- **Li-ion:** graphite anode (LiC₆), metal-oxide cathode (LiCoO₂, LiFePO₄, NMC), organic electrolyte with LiPF₆; ~3.6–3.7 V; Li⁺ shuttles between electrodes (rocking-chair).
- **Ni–MH, Ni–Cd** (older).

steps.title: Fuel cells
steps.body: Convert fuel's chemical energy directly into electricity while fuel is supplied. H₂–O₂ (alkaline/PEM): anode H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (PEM); cathode ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O; E° ≈ 1.23 V. Product is water; efficiency higher than heat engines (not Carnot-limited).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 12 V car battery = 6 lead–acid cells in series.

**Example 2.** Energy of a 3.7 V, 3000 mAh phone battery: 3.7 × 3 = 11.1 Wh = 40 kJ.

**Example 3.** H₂–O₂ fuel cell ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96500 × 1.23 ≈ −237 kJ per mol H₂.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling fuel cells batteries (they don't store reactants internally).
- Forgetting Li-ion safety: overcharge or puncture can cause thermal runaway — use proper chargers and BMS.
- Mixing mAh with Wh (multiply by voltage).

quiz.why: A single lead–acid cell gives about 2 V. A 12 V battery has six cells in series.

quiz.q: During discharge of lead–acid, acid density
quiz.why: On discharge sulphuric acid is used up and water is formed, so the acid becomes more dilute and its density falls.
In a lithium-ion cell the anode is graphite, where lithium is stored as LiC₆.
The standard EMF of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is 1.23 V, from E°(O₂/H₂O) − E°(H⁺/H₂).
Primary cells cannot be recharged, since the reactions are not reversible in practice. Secondary cells can be recharged.

scenes.text: Steel railings near the sea rust far faster than those inland.
Moisture, salt and oxygen create electrochemical cells on the metal surface.

steps.title: Dry (chemical) corrosion
steps.body: Direct attack by gases (O₂, Cl₂, H₂S) at high temperature. Oxide film type decides further attack — **Pilling–Bedworth ratio** = volume of oxide/volume of metal: < 1 porous (Li, Na, K — continue to corrode), 1–2 protective (Al, Cr), > 2 may crack.

steps.title: Wet (electrochemical) corrosion
steps.body:
Anodic area: M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻ (metal dissolves).
Cathodic area: O₂ absorption (neutral/alkaline): O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻; or H₂ evolution (acidic): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
Rust: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂ → oxidised to Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
- **Galvanic corrosion:** two dissimilar metals in contact — the more active (anodic) one corrodes (e.g. steel bolt on copper sheet).
- **Differential aeration:** less-oxygenated part becomes anode (pitting, waterline, crevice corrosion).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Zinc-coated iron scratched: Zn is anodic and corrodes, iron protected (galvanising). Tin-coated iron scratched: iron is anodic and corrodes fast at the scratch.

**Example 2.** A small anode with a large cathode corrodes intensely — so never use steel rivets on copper sheets (small anode); copper rivets on steel are safer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the oxygen-rich region corrodes in differential aeration (it is the oxygen-poor region).
- Ignoring area ratio in galvanic corrosion.
- Thinking pure metals never corrode.

statements.s: In differential aeration, the less aerated area is anodic.
A scratched tin-plated can protects the iron below.
Pilling–Bedworth ratio < 1 gives a protective film.
Galvanising uses zinc as a sacrificial coat.

quiz.why: Rust is hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

quiz.q: Cathodic reaction in neutral aerated water
quiz.why: In neutral aerated water the cathodic reaction is oxygen reduction: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Hydrogen evolution occurs in acidic media.
In galvanic corrosion the more active (anodic) metal of a couple corrodes, and the nobler metal is protected.
Pitting is localised attack, often due to differential aeration, where a poorly oxygenated spot becomes anodic.
Aluminium forms a thin, adherent, protective oxide (Al₂O₃) film, which passivates the surface.
options: it forms a protective oxide film

scenes.text: A buried oil pipeline runs 500 km through damp soil.
Engineers use coatings plus cathodic protection to make it last decades.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body: Metal: position in galvanic series, purity, area ratio, oxide film, overvoltage. Environment: temperature, humidity, pH (acidic faster), dissolved O₂, chlorides, conductivity.

steps.title: Protection methods
steps.body:
- **Design:** avoid dissimilar-metal contact, crevices; insulate joints; drainage.
- **Cathodic protection:** sacrificial anode (Mg, Zn blocks) or impressed current (DC source, inert anode).
- **Coatings:** metallic — anodic (galvanising Zn) or cathodic (tinning Sn, chrome, nickel); electroplating; inorganic (phosphating, anodising Al); organic (paints, epoxy).
- **Inhibitors:** anodic (chromates, phosphates), cathodic (Zn salts, amines), vapour-phase.
- **Material selection:** stainless steel (≥ 10.5% Cr) forms passive Cr₂O₃.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Ship hull: Zn or Mg blocks bolted on — sacrificial anodes replaced periodically.

**Example 2.** Why galvanised (not tinned) iron for water tanks but tinned iron for food cans? Zn salts are toxic in acidic foods; tin is non-toxic though only protective when unbroken.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Cu as a sacrificial anode for steel (Cu is nobler).
- Painting only the anode area of a galvanic couple (it concentrates attack at defects — paint the cathode too).
- Forgetting that impressed-current systems need continuous monitoring.

quiz.why: A sacrificial anode must be more active than steel. Magnesium is more active, so it corrodes in place of the steel.
Tin is nobler than iron, so tinning is a cathodic coating: it protects only while the coating is unbroken. At a scratch the iron corrodes faster.

quiz.q: Stainless steel resists corrosion due to
quiz.why: Stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin, self-healing Cr₂O₃ passive film.
Corrosion usually speeds up with higher temperature and acidity (and moisture and dissolved salts).
Anodising thickens the protective oxide layer on aluminium by electrolytic oxidation, making Al₂O₃.

questions.q: Nernst equation relates EMF to
questions.why: The Nernst equation relates cell potential to the concentrations (activities) of the species.

questions.q: Rechargeable battery is
questions.why: The lead–acid battery is a secondary (rechargeable) battery. Dry cells and mercury or alkaline primary cells cannot be recharged.

questions.q: Galvanising coats iron with
questions.why: Galvanising coats iron or steel with zinc, which gives sacrificial protection.

questions.q: Cathode in a galvanic cell
questions.why: At the cathode of a galvanic cell reduction takes place, and it is the positive terminal.

questions.q: E for Zn²⁺/Zn at 0.01 M (E° = −0.76)
Fuel cell advantage
questions.why: A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electricity, so it is not Carnot-limited, giving high efficiency and a clean product (water for H₂).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Iron rivets on a copper plate corrode rapidly.  Reason (R): Small anodic area with large cathodic area intensifies corrosion.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: iron is the anode and copper the cathode. A small anode with a large cathode means the whole corrosion current is concentrated on a small area, so iron corrodes rapidly.

questions.q: Pilling–Bedworth ratio for Al ≈ 1.28 ⇒ film
questions.why: The Pilling–Bedworth ratio between 1 and 2 means the oxide is slightly larger than the metal it replaces and forms a compact, protective film. Al, at about 1.28, is protective.

questions.q: Equilibrium constant for E° = 0.0591 V, n = 1 at 298 K
Concentration cell 0.001 M | 0.1 M Ag⁺/Ag EMF
questions.why: For a concentration cell E = (0.0591/n) log(C₂/C₁) = 0.0591 × log(0.1/0.001) = 0.0591 × 2 = 0.118 V.

questions.q: Case: A steel water tank fitted with zinc anodes loses 2 kg Zn per year. If Zn is removed, the tank
questions.why: Zinc anodes protect the steel tank by sacrificial action. Without them the tank loses this protection and begins corroding.

questions.q: Energy (Wh) of a 48 V, 30 Ah e-bike pack
questions.why: Energy (Wh) = voltage × capacity (Ah) = 48 × 30 = 1440 Wh.

questions.q: ΔG° for E° = 1.5 V, n = 2
Waterline corrosion occurs just
questions.why: In waterline corrosion the metal just below the waterline has less oxygen than that just above it, so it becomes anodic and corrodes (differential aeration).

questions.q: pH from glass electrode: E = 0.0591 × pH (relative). E = 0.413 V ⇒ pH

courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 3 · Polymers and engineering plastics
courses.summary: Classification of polymers, addition and condensation polymerisation, degree of polymerisation and molecular mass, thermoplastics and thermosets, preparation and uses of key polymers, elastomers and vulcanisation, conducting and biodegradable polymers, and composites.
outcomes: Classify polymers and polymerisation mechanisms
Compute degree of polymerisation and average molecular masses
Describe preparation, properties and uses of common plastics and rubbers
Explain conducting, biodegradable polymers and fibre-reinforced composites
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: PET bottles, nylon ropes, Kevlar vests — all polymers.
Small monomers link into chains thousands of units long.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: By origin (natural/synthetic), structure (linear, branched, cross-linked), tacticity (isotactic, syndiotactic, atactic), composition (homo/copolymer), behaviour on heating (thermoplastic/thermoset), mechanism (addition/condensation).

steps.title: Mechanisms
steps.body:
- **Addition (chain-growth):** monomers with C=C; initiation (free radical from benzoyl peroxide), propagation, termination; no by-product (PE, PVC, PS, PTFE).
- **Condensation (step-growth):** bifunctional monomers react with loss of small molecules (H₂O, HCl) — nylon-6,6, polyesters, Bakelite.
- **Functionality:** number of reactive sites; f = 2 gives linear, f ≥ 3 gives cross-linked network.
- **Degree of polymerisation** DP = M(polymer)/M(repeat unit).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Polyethylene of M = 28 000 g/mol: DP = 28 000/28 = 1000.

**Example 2.** Mn vs Mw: 10 molecules of 10 000 and 10 of 30 000 g/mol. Mn = (10×10⁴ + 10×3×10⁴)/20 = 20 000. Mw = Σnᵢ Mᵢ²/Σnᵢ Mᵢ = (10×10⁸ + 10×9×10⁸)/(4×10⁵) = 25 000. PDI = 1.25.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling nylon an addition polymer (it is condensation).
- Thinking PDI < 1 is possible (Mw ≥ Mn).
- Forgetting that a bifunctional monomer cannot form a 3-D network alone.

quiz.why: Addition polymerisation needs monomers with a C=C double bond (unsaturation), which opens up to join the chain.

quiz.q: DP of PVC with M = 62 500 (repeat unit 62.5)
quiz.why: Degree of polymerisation = molar mass of polymer/molar mass of repeat unit = 62,500/62.5 = 1000.
The ratio Mw/Mn is the polydispersity index (PDI), which is a measure of the spread of chain lengths.
A cross-linked network needs monomers with functionality of 3 or more, so chains can branch and link in 3-D.
Benzoyl peroxide is a common free-radical initiator, since it splits into radicals on heating.

story.title: Why a pan handle is Bakelite

scenes.text: A frying pan's handle is Bakelite; its packaging film is polyethylene.
One softens on heating, the other chars — structure decides.

steps.title: Thermoplastic vs thermoset
steps.body:
Thermoplastics: linear/branched chains held by weak forces; soften on heating, recyclable (PE, PP, PVC, PS, PET, nylon).
Thermosets: 3-D cross-linked; set permanently on curing; do not soften, char on strong heating (Bakelite, epoxy, urea–formaldehyde).

steps.title: Key polymers
steps.body:
- **PE:** LDPE (high pressure, branched, films), HDPE (Ziegler–Natta, linear, pipes).
- **PVC:** vinyl chloride; plasticised for cables, rigid for pipes.
- **PTFE (Teflon):** very inert, low friction, non-stick coatings.
- **PMMA:** transparent sheets (acrylic).
- **Nylon-6,6:** hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid; fibres, gears.
- **PET:** ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid; bottles, fibres.
- **Bakelite:** phenol + formaldehyde (novolac → cured with hexamine); electrical switches.
- **Epoxy:** bisphenol-A + epichlorohydrin; adhesives, composites.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Why is PTFE non-stick? Strong C–F bonds and fully fluorinated surface give very low surface energy.

**Example 2.** Why is HDPE stiffer than LDPE? Linear chains pack better ⇒ higher crystallinity and density.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying thermosets can be remoulded.
- Mixing up monomers of nylon-6,6 and nylon-6 (caprolactam).
- Calling Teflon a thermoset (it is a thermoplastic, though hard to melt-process).

quiz.why: Bakelite is a thermosetting plastic with a rigid 3-D cross-linked network. Polyethylene, PVC and nylon are thermoplastics.
High-density polyethylene (HDPE) is made at low pressure with a Ziegler–Natta catalyst, giving linear chains. LDPE is made by high-pressure free-radical polymerisation.
PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate, plexiglass) is the transparent acrylic sheet.
Thermoplastics have weak secondary forces between chains, so they soften on heating and can be remoulded.
PTFE (Teflon) is used for non-stick coatings, because of its inert, low-friction C–F surface.

scenes.text: Natural rubber gets sticky in summer and brittle in winter.
Goodyear's vulcanisation with sulphur made car tyres possible.

steps.title: Natural and synthetic rubber
steps.body:
Natural rubber = cis-1,4-polyisoprene from latex; elastic because coiled chains uncoil under stress and recoil. Drawbacks: low tensile strength, tacky when hot, brittle when cold, swells in oils.
**Vulcanisation:** heating with 3–5% sulphur forms S cross-links between chains at allylic positions — stronger, less tacky, wider temperature range. High sulphur (~30%) gives hard ebonite.

steps.title: Synthetic elastomers
steps.body:
- **Buna-S (SBR):** butadiene + styrene — tyres.
- **Buna-N (nitrile):** butadiene + acrylonitrile — oil-resistant hoses, seals.
- **Neoprene:** chloroprene — oil and weather resistant.
- **Silicone rubber:** –Si–O– backbone — high temperature, medical uses.
- **Polyurethane:** foams, coatings.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Choose a rubber for an oil seal in a pump: Buna-N or neoprene (oil resistant), not natural rubber.

**Example 2.** Why does a stretched rubber band warm up? Stretching aligns chains (entropy decreases), releasing heat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more sulphur always helps (too much makes it brittle — ebonite).
- Confusing gutta-percha (trans-polyisoprene, hard) with natural rubber (cis).
- Using natural rubber with petrol/oil.

quiz.why: Buna-S (SBR) is made from butadiene and styrene.
Rubber is vulcanised by heating with sulphur, which makes cross-links between chains.
Neoprene is made by polymerising chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene).
Silicone rubber has an inorganic Si–O (siloxane) backbone.

quiz.q: Elasticity of rubber is due to
quiz.why: Rubber is elastic because its coiled chains uncoil on stretching and recoil when released, which is driven by entropy.

scenes.text: Foldable displays and OLEDs use conducting polymers.
Meanwhile, compostable cutlery uses PLA, a biodegradable polymer.

steps.title: Conducting polymers
steps.body: Conjugated backbones (alternating single–double bonds): polyacetylene, polyaniline, polypyrrole, polythiophene, PEDOT:PSS. Doping (oxidation: p-type with I₂; reduction: n-type with Na) creates charge carriers (polarons/bipolarons). Nobel Prize 2000 (Heeger, MacDiarmid, Shirakawa). Uses: OLEDs, antistatic coatings, sensors, batteries.

steps.title: Biodegradable polymers and composites
steps.body:
Biodegradable: PLA (polylactic acid), PHB/PHBV (bacterial polyesters), PGA, starch blends — degrade by hydrolysis/microbes.
**Composites:** matrix (polymer/metal/ceramic) + reinforcement (glass, carbon, aramid fibres). FRP: high strength-to-weight, corrosion resistance — aircraft, wind blades, boats. Rule of mixtures: E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m (longitudinal).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Carbon fibre/epoxy with V_f = 0.6, E_f = 230 GPa, E_m = 3.5 GPa: E_c = 138 + 1.4 = 139.4 GPa.

**Example 2.** Glass fibre (72 GPa) at V_f = 0.4 in polyester (3 GPa): E_c = 28.8 + 1.8 = 30.6 GPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all plastics labelled 'bio-based' are biodegradable.
- Applying the rule of mixtures to the transverse direction (it overestimates).
- Forgetting that undoped polyacetylene is a poor conductor.

activity.prompt: Composite: E_f = 200 GPa, V_f = 0.5, E_m = 4 GPa. Longitudinal modulus (GPa)?

quiz.why: Conducting polymers need a conjugated backbone (alternating single and double bonds) and doping to create mobile charge carriers.
PLA (polylactic acid) is a biodegradable polymer, a polyester that microbes can break down.
FRP stands for fibre-reinforced polymer, a composite of strong fibres in a polymer matrix.
The rule of mixtures for longitudinal modulus (iso-strain) is E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m.
Polyaniline becomes conducting when doped with acid (protonated emeraldine salt form).

questions.q: Monomer of polyethylene
questions.why: The monomer of polyethylene is ethylene (CH₂=CH₂).

questions.q: Nylon-6,6 is formed by
questions.why: Nylon-6,6 is formed by condensation polymerisation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, with water lost.

questions.q: Thermoplastics can be
questions.why: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded repeatedly.

questions.q: DP of polystyrene M = 104 000 (repeat 104)
Which is an elastomer?
questions.why: Neoprene is a synthetic rubber (an elastomer). PET and PMMA are thermoplastics and Bakelite is a thermoset.

questions.q: Catalyst for HDPE / isotactic PP
questions.why: Ziegler–Natta catalysts (TiCl₄ with an alkyl-aluminium) give HDPE and isotactic polypropylene.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Bakelite cannot be remoulded.  Reason (R): It has a 3-D cross-linked network.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: Bakelite has a 3-D cross-linked network, which cannot soften or flow on heating, so it cannot be remoulded.

questions.q: Mn of 5 chains of 20 000 and 5 of 40 000
Mw of the same mixture
Oil-resistant elastomer for fuel hoses
questions.why: Buna-N (nitrile rubber) resists oils and fuels, so it is used for fuel hoses and seals.

questions.q: Case: An aircraft panel needs high stiffness and low weight. Best choice
questions.why: A carbon-fibre/epoxy composite has very high stiffness and strength for its low weight (high specific modulus), which suits aircraft panels.

questions.q: E_c for glass fibre 70 GPa, V_f = 0.5, matrix 3 GPa
Polyacetylene becomes metallic-like on doping with
questions.why: Polyacetylene is doped with iodine (p-doping, oxidation), which creates charge carriers and makes it metal-like.

questions.q: Polymer with highest chemical inertness
questions.why: PTFE has the strong, shielded C–F bonds, so it is highly inert chemically.

questions.q: A polymer with PDI = 1 is
questions.why: A PDI of 1 (Mw = Mn) means all chains have the same length, so the polymer is monodisperse.

courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 4 · Fuels and combustion
courses.summary: Classification and calorific value of fuels, bomb calorimeter and Dulong's formula, proximate and ultimate analysis of coal, petroleum refining, cracking, knocking, octane and cetane numbers, gaseous fuels and combustion calculations.
outcomes: Calculate gross and net calorific values
Interpret proximate and ultimate analysis of coal
Explain refining, cracking, knocking, octane and cetane numbers
Compute air required for combustion
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A plant manager compares coal, LPG and biomass for a boiler.
The calorific value — heat per kg — is the first number to check.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**HCV/GCV:** heat released when unit mass burns completely and products cool to room temperature (water vapour condenses).
**LCV/NCV:** HCV minus latent heat of the water formed: LCV = HCV − 0.09 H × 587 cal/g (H in %; 9 g water per g of H; latent heat 587 cal/g).

steps.title: Bomb calorimeter and Dulong
steps.body:
Bomb calorimeter (solid/liquid): HCV = (W + w)(t₂ − t₁)/x, where W = water mass, w = water equivalent, x = fuel mass; corrections for fuse wire, acid formation and cooling.
Dulong's formula: HCV = (1/100)[8080 C + 34500 (H − O/8) + 2240 S] kcal/kg (C, H, O, S in %). Boys' gas calorimeter for gaseous fuels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 9H without the 0.09 (percentage) factor.
- Forgetting O/8 (oxygen already 'combined' with some hydrogen).
- Mixing kcal/kg and kJ/kg (1 kcal = 4.187 kJ).

quiz.why: The higher calorific value (HCV) includes the latent heat released when the water vapour formed condenses.

quiz.q: Water formed per g of hydrogen
quiz.why: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 4 g of H₂ gives 36 g of water, so 1 g of H₂ gives 9 g.
A bomb calorimeter measures the calorific value of solid and liquid fuels (burnt in oxygen at constant volume).

quiz.q: In Dulong's formula, available hydrogen is
quiz.why: In Dulong's formula, part of the hydrogen is already combined with oxygen as water, so the available hydrogen is H − O/8.
LCV = HCV − latent heat of the water formed, so LCV is always less than HCV.

story.title: Buying coal for a power plant

scenes.text: A thermal plant receives rakes of coal with different ash content.
Proximate analysis decides price and boiler settings.

steps.title: Proximate analysis
steps.body:
- **Moisture:** heat 1 g at 105–110 °C for 1 h. % = loss/mass × 100.
- **Volatile matter:** moisture-free sample in a covered crucible at 925 ± 5 °C for 7 min.
- **Ash:** heat uncovered at 700–750 °C until constant mass.
- **Fixed carbon** = 100 − (M + VM + A).
High moisture/ash lower CV; high VM gives long smoky flame; high fixed carbon = high CV.

steps.title: Ultimate analysis and ranks
steps.body:
Elements C, H, N, S, O: C and H by combustion (CO₂ absorbed in KOH, H₂O in CaCl₂/anhydrone); N by Kjeldahl; S by BaSO₄ precipitation; O by difference.
Rank order (increasing C and CV): peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite. Coking coal for metallurgy; carbonisation gives coke (low-temperature and high-temperature).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 2.5 g coal loses 0.15 g at 110 °C: moisture = 0.15/2.5 × 100 = 6%. If the dried sample then loses a further 0.75 g at 925 °C, VM = 0.75/2.5 × 100 = 30%; residue after ignition 0.25 g ⇒ ash 10%; fixed carbon = 100 − 46 = 54%.

**Example 2.** 1 g coal in Kjeldahl's method: NH₃ neutralised 3 mL of 0.1 N H₂SO₄ ⇒ %N = (1.4 × V × N)/W = 1.4 × 3 × 0.1/1 = 0.42%.

**Example 3.** 0.5 g coal gives 0.05 g BaSO₄ ⇒ %S = (32/233)(0.05/0.5)(100) = 1.37%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Determining VM on a sample that still contains moisture.
- Calculating fixed carbon without subtracting all three.
- Using 14 instead of 1.4 in the Kjeldahl % formula.

quiz.why: Fixed carbon = 100 − (moisture + volatile matter + ash), by difference in proximate analysis.
Anthracite is the highest rank of coal, with the most carbon and the least volatile matter and moisture.

quiz.q: Nitrogen in coal is found by
quiz.why: Nitrogen in coal is found by Kjeldahl's method, converting it to ammonia and titrating.
Ash is inert, so a high ash content lowers the calorific value and causes disposal problems.
Volatile matter is determined by heating a covered crucible at 925 ± 20 °C for 7 minutes.

lessons.title: Petroleum, cracking, knocking and fuel ratings

story.title: Why petrol has an octane number

scenes.text: Petrol pumps sell 91 and 95 octane fuels.
Higher octane resists knocking — essential for high-compression engines.

steps.title: Refining and cracking
steps.body: Fractional distillation of crude: LPG, petrol (40–120 °C), naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oils, residue. **Cracking** breaks heavy molecules into lighter, more useful ones: thermal cracking, catalytic cracking (zeolites/alumina-silica; more branched, higher-octane petrol), hydrocracking.

steps.title: Knocking and ratings
steps.body:
**Knocking (SI engines):** premature self-ignition of the end gas ⇒ metallic sound, power loss, damage. Resistance: branched alkanes > olefins > cycloalkanes > straight-chain alkanes.
**Octane number** = % iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane, ON 100) in a mixture with n-heptane (ON 0) that knocks like the fuel. Improvers: MTBE, ethanol (TEL now banned).
**Cetane number (CI/diesel):** % n-cetane (hexadecane, CN 100) in mixture with α-methylnaphthalene (CN 0). Straight chains ignite easily ⇒ high CN — opposite trend to octane.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A fuel knocks like 80% iso-octane + 20% n-heptane ⇒ ON = 80.

**Example 2.** Why is a good petrol a poor diesel? Branched molecules resist self-ignition (high ON) but diesel needs easy self-ignition (high CN).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying high octane fuel has more energy (it resists knock; CV similar).
- Reversing the structure trends of ON and CN.
- Calling TEL a current additive (phased out for health reasons).

quiz.why: Knocking is premature auto-ignition of the end gas in spark-ignition (petrol) engines.
Branched alkanes (like iso-octane) resist knocking, so high-octane fuels contain more of them.
A good diesel fuel has a high cetane number, meaning it ignites readily under compression.
Cracking breaks heavy, high-boiling oil fractions into lighter, more useful ones such as petrol.

quiz.q: Fuel equivalent to 70% iso-octane + 30% n-heptane has ON
quiz.why: The octane number is the percentage of iso-octane in the iso-octane/n-heptane blend that matches the fuel's knocking, so 70% iso-octane gives ON 70.

scenes.text: A furnace engineer must size the air blower for burning coal.
Stoichiometry gives the minimum air; excess air is added for complete burning.

steps.title: Gaseous fuels
steps.body: LPG (propane + butane, ~11 000 kcal/kg), CNG (mainly methane, ~200 bar storage), producer gas (CO + N₂, low CV), water gas (CO + H₂), biogas (CH₄ + CO₂), hydrogen (highest CV per kg, ~34 000 kcal/kg).

steps.title: Combustion calculations
steps.body:
C + O₂ → CO₂ (12 g C needs 32 g O₂); 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (4 g H₂ needs 32 g O₂); S + O₂ → SO₂.
O₂ needed per kg fuel = (32/12)C + 8(H − O/8) + S (masses in kg). Air = O₂ × 100/23 (by mass) or by volume: O₂ × 100/21. Add excess air %.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Coal C 80%, H 5%, O 4%, S 1% per kg: O₂ = (32/12)(0.80) + 8(0.05 − 0.005) + 0.01 = 2.133 + 0.36 + 0.01 = 2.503 kg. Air = 2.503 × 100/23 = 10.88 kg; with 25% excess = 13.6 kg.

**Example 2.** 1 m³ methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O ⇒ 2 m³ O₂ ⇒ air = 2 × 100/21 = 9.52 m³.

**Example 3.** Orsat apparatus analyses flue gas for CO₂ (KOH), O₂ (alkaline pyrogallol), CO (ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂) in that order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 21% (volume) for mass calculations — use 23% by mass.
- Forgetting to subtract oxygen already in the fuel.
- Wrong order of absorbents in Orsat.

activity.prompt: Volume of air (m³) for complete combustion of 1 m³ of CO (2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂)? Use 21% O₂.

quiz.q: Air needed per kg O₂ (mass basis)
quiz.why: Air is about 23% oxygen by mass, so 1 kg of oxygen comes with 100/23 kg of air.
C + O₂ → CO₂: 12 kg of carbon needs 32 kg of O₂, so 1 kg needs 32/12 = 2.67 kg.
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: 4 kg of H₂ needs 32 kg of O₂, so 1 kg needs 8 kg.
Compressed natural gas (CNG) is mainly methane.
In an Orsat apparatus, CO₂ is absorbed first, in KOH solution. Then O₂ is absorbed by alkaline pyrogallol, and CO by cuprous chloride.

questions.q: LPG mainly contains
questions.why: LPG consists mainly of propane and butane.

questions.q: HCV − LCV equals the
questions.why: HCV − LCV equals the latent heat of the steam (water) formed, as it is recovered in HCV.

questions.q: Coal with highest moisture
questions.why: Peat is the lowest-rank coal, with the highest moisture content.

questions.q: Octane number of n-heptane
questions.why: By definition, n-heptane has an octane number of 0 and iso-octane has 100.

questions.q: Fixed carbon for M 5%, VM 30%, A 15%
Air volume for 1 m³ CH₄ (21% O₂)
questions.why: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O needs 2 m³ of O₂, which is in 2/0.21 = 9.52 m³ of air.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Straight-chain hydrocarbons make good diesel fuels.  Reason (R): They self-ignite readily under compression.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: straight-chain hydrocarbons self-ignite easily under compression, which is what a diesel engine needs, giving a high cetane number.

questions.q: Dulong HCV for C 85%, H 5%, O 8%, S 0
Bomb calorimeter: W + w = 3000 g, Δt = 2 °C, x = 0.75 g ⇒ HCV
Kjeldahl: 2 g coal, 5 mL of 0.1 N acid ⇒ %N
questions.why: %N = 1.4 × normality × volume of acid/mass = 1.4 × 0.1 × 5/2 = 0.35%.

questions.q: Case: Coal C 90%, H 3%, O 2% (rest ash). Theoretical air per kg (mass)
Same coal with 30% excess air
questions.why: Actual air = theoretical × 1.3 = 11.4 × 1.3 ≈ 14.8 kg.

questions.q: Main product of catalytic cracking beneficial for petrol
questions.why: Catalytic cracking produces branched alkanes and aromatics, which have high octane numbers and so make better petrol.

questions.q: Fuel with highest calorific value per kg
questions.why: Hydrogen has by far the highest calorific value per kg, about 34,000 kcal/kg (coal ≈ 6000–8000).

questions.q: LCV for HCV 10 000 kcal/kg, H 10%

courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 5 · Spectroscopy and analytical techniques
courses.summary: Electromagnetic spectrum and Beer–Lambert law, UV–visible spectroscopy and chromophores, IR spectroscopy and functional groups, NMR basics (chemical shift, splitting), and chromatography and conductometric/pH titrations.
outcomes: Apply the Beer–Lambert law
Interpret UV–Vis transitions and λmax shifts
Identify functional groups from IR bands
Read simple ¹H NMR spectra; describe chromatography and instrumental titrations
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A lab measures iron in drinking water by how much coloured complex absorbs light.
Absorbance rises linearly with concentration — Beer–Lambert.

steps.title: Beer–Lambert law
steps.body: A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl, ε = molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), c (mol/L), l (cm). Transmittance T = I/I₀; A = −log T. Valid for dilute solutions and monochromatic light.

steps.title: Electronic transitions
steps.body:
σ→σ* (< 200 nm), n→σ*, π→π* (strong, conjugated systems), n→π* (weak, carbonyls ~280 nm).
Chromophore: group causing absorption (C=C, C=O, N=N). Auxochrome: modifies it (–OH, –NH₂).
Shifts: bathochromic (red, longer λ), hypsochromic (blue), hyperchromic (more intense), hypochromic. More conjugation ⇒ longer λmax (β-carotene is orange).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ε = 1.2×10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm, A = 0.6 ⇒ c = 0.6/1.2×10⁴ = 5×10⁻⁵ M.

**Example 2.** T = 10% ⇒ A = 1. T = 50% ⇒ A = 0.301.

**Example 3.** Ethylene absorbs ~171 nm; butadiene ~217 nm; hexatriene ~258 nm — conjugation shifts λmax to the red.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln instead of log₁₀.
- Expecting linearity at high concentrations.
- Confusing absorbance with transmittance (%T).

activity.prompt: A = 0.45, ε = 9000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm. Concentration in µmol/L?

quiz.why: The Beer–Lambert law is A = εcl: absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.
More conjugation lowers the energy gap, so λ_max moves to longer wavelength, a bathochromic (red) shift.
An auxochrome (such as –OH or –NH₂) is a group that modifies the absorption of a chromophore. C=O, C=C and N=N are chromophores.

quiz.q: Weak band of ketones ~280 nm is
quiz.why: The weak band of ketones near 280 nm is the n → π* transition.

scenes.text: A recycling lab must tell polyester from nylon quickly.
An IR spectrum shows C=O near 1730 cm⁻¹ for polyester and amide bands for nylon.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
IR (4000–400 cm⁻¹) excites molecular vibrations. A vibration is IR-active only if it changes the dipole moment (so N₂, O₂ are inactive; CO₂ asymmetric stretch is active).
Number of vibrational modes: 3N − 6 (non-linear), 3N − 5 (linear).
Wavenumber ν̄ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ): stronger bond or lighter atoms ⇒ higher wavenumber.

steps.title: Characteristic bands
steps.body:
- O–H (alcohol) 3200–3600 (broad); carboxylic O–H 2500–3300 (very broad)
- N–H 3300–3500
- C–H 2850–3000 (sp³), ~3030–3100 (sp²), ~3300 (sp)
- C≡N ~2250; C≡C ~2100–2260
- C=O 1650–1800 (ketone ~1715, ester ~1735, amide ~1650)
- C=C ~1600–1680
- Fingerprint region below 1500 cm⁻¹ — unique to each molecule.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H₂O (non-linear, N = 3): 3 modes; CO₂ (linear): 4 modes.

**Example 2.** A compound shows a broad band at 3300 and strong band at 1050 cm⁻¹, no C=O ⇒ an alcohol.

**Example 3.** Band at 1715 and none at 3300 ⇒ ketone (not acid).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting homonuclear diatomics to absorb IR.
- Forgetting the linear-molecule formula 3N − 5.
- Over-interpreting the fingerprint region in simple exam questions.

quiz.why: A non-linear molecule has 3N − 6 vibrational modes. For CH₄ (N = 5): 15 − 6 = 9.
N₂ is homonuclear, so its stretching causes no change in dipole moment and it is IR-inactive.
Heavier atoms increase the reduced mass, so the stretching frequency (wavenumber) is lower.
The fingerprint region, below about 1500 cm⁻¹, has a complex pattern unique to each molecule.
The C=O stretching band appears strongly at 1650–1800 cm⁻¹.

scenes.text: An MRI scanner maps hydrogen nuclei in the body.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Nuclei with spin (¹H, ¹³C) in a magnetic field B₀ absorb radio waves at resonance. Electron shielding shifts resonance: **chemical shift** δ (ppm) relative to TMS (δ = 0).
Typical δ: alkyl C–H 0.9–1.5; next to C=O 2–2.5; O–CH 3.3–4; vinyl 4.5–6.5; aromatic 6.5–8; aldehyde 9–10; carboxylic 10–12.

steps.title: Reading a spectrum
steps.body:
- Number of signals = number of chemically distinct H environments.
- Integration ∝ number of H in each.
- Splitting (n + 1 rule): a signal is split into n + 1 lines by n equivalent neighbouring H (doublet, triplet, quartet).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH: 3 signals; CH₃ triplet (δ ~1.2, 3H), CH₂ quartet (~3.6, 2H), OH singlet (variable, 1H).

**Example 2.** Acetone: one singlet at δ ≈ 2.1 (6 equivalent H).

**Example 3.** Benzene: one singlet at δ ≈ 7.3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting equivalent H separately.
- Applying n + 1 to protons on the same carbon (equivalent H don't split each other).
- Forgetting TMS is the reference at 0 ppm.

activity.text: The CH₃ signal is a ___ (split by 2 H) and the CH₂ signal is a ___ (split by 3 H).

quiz.why: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is the standard reference in NMR, defined as δ = 0.
All six hydrogens in acetone, CH₃COCH₃, are equivalent, so there is a single signal.

quiz.q: A CH₂ next to CH₃ appears as a
quiz.why: By the n + 1 rule, a CH₂ next to a CH₃ (3 neighbouring H) is split into 3 + 1 = 4 lines, a quartet.
The aldehyde proton is strongly deshielded by the carbonyl group, so it appears at δ 9–10 ppm.
The integration (area under a signal) gives the relative number of protons giving that signal.

steps.title: Chromatography
steps.body: Separation by distribution between a stationary and a mobile phase. Paper/TLC: Rf = distance by solute/distance by solvent (0–1). Column, GC (volatile samples, carrier gas), HPLC (high-pressure liquid). Identification by retention time; quantity by peak area.

steps.title: Conductometric and pH titrations
steps.body:
**Conductometric:** conductance vs volume. Strong acid + strong base: falls (H⁺ replaced by slower Na⁺) then rises (excess OH⁻) — V shape; end point at the minimum. Weak acid + strong base: slow rise then steeper rise.
**pH-metric:** sharp jump at equivalence (strong–strong around pH 7); for weak acid, pH at half-equivalence = pKa.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spot travels 3.0 cm, solvent 7.5 cm: Rf = 0.40.

**Example 2.** pH at half-neutralisation of acetic acid = pKa = 4.76.

**Example 3.** 25 mL HCl needs 20 mL 0.1 M NaOH (minimum in conductance) ⇒ [HCl] = 0.08 M.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rf > 1 (impossible — check measurements).
- Expecting a sharp minimum for weak acid conductometric titrations.
- Forgetting temperature control (conductance changes ~2% per °C).

quiz.q: pH at half-equivalence of weak acid
quiz.why: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻], so by Henderson–Hasselbalch pH = pKa.

lessons.title: Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws and resistor networks

scenes.text: An electrician finds one lamp in a string dark and wonders if the others are series or parallel.
KCL and KVL tell exactly what current flows where.

steps.title: Basic laws
steps.body:
Ohm: V = IR; power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Resistance R = ρL/A, R_T = R₀(1 + α₀T).
**KCL:** Σ currents entering a node = 0 (charge conservation).
**KVL:** Σ voltages around a closed loop = 0 (energy conservation).
Series R_eq = ΣR (same current, voltage divides: Vₖ = V Rₖ/R_eq). Parallel 1/R_eq = Σ1/R (same voltage, current divides: I₁ = I R₂/(R₁ + R₂)).

steps.title: Star–delta transformation
steps.body:
Δ → Y: R_a = R_ab R_ca/(R_ab + R_bc + R_ca) (product of adjacent / sum).
Y → Δ: R_ab = R_a + R_b + R_aR_b/R_c (sum of two + their product / third).
Equal resistors: R_Y = R_Δ/3.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4 Ω in series with (6 ∥ 3) across 12 V: 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω ⇒ R = 6 Ω, I = 2 A; current in 6 Ω = 2 × 3/9 = 0.667 A.

**Example 2.** Δ of 30 Ω each → Y of 10 Ω each.

**Example 3.** A 100 W, 230 V lamp: R = V²/P = 529 Ω; I = 0.435 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inconsistent sign conventions in KVL (choose a direction and stick to it).
- Adding parallel resistances directly.
- Using star–delta formulas the wrong way round.

quiz.q: KCL is based on conservation of
quiz.why: Kirchhoff's current law says the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero, which expresses conservation of charge.
Two equal resistors in parallel give half: 10/2 = 5 Ω.

quiz.q: Δ of 9 Ω each converts to Y of
quiz.why: A delta of equal resistors R converts to a star of R/3 each: 9/3 = 3 Ω.

quiz.why: In a series circuit there is only one path, so the same current flows through every element.

lessons.title: Mesh and nodal analysis

scenes.text: An engineer must find the current in a bridge resistor of a sensor circuit.
Mesh or nodal analysis gives a set of linear equations — solved systematically.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Mesh (loop) analysis:** assign clockwise mesh currents; write KVL for each mesh; shared resistors carry the difference of mesh currents. Number of equations = number of independent meshes.
**Nodal analysis:** choose a reference node; write KCL at other nodes with currents (V_node − V_other)/R. Number of equations = nodes − 1.
Supermesh (current source between meshes) and supernode (voltage source between nodes) handle sources.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (mesh).** 10 V source, R₁ = 2 Ω in mesh 1, shared R₂ = 4 Ω, R₃ = 6 Ω in mesh 2 (no source).
Mesh 1: 10 = 6I₁ − 4I₂. Mesh 2: 0 = −4I₁ + 10I₂ ⇒ I₁ = 2.5I₂ ⇒ 10 = 15I₂ − 4I₂ = 11I₂ ⇒ I₂ = 0.909 A, I₁ = 2.273 A. Current in R₂ = 1.364 A.

**Example 2 (nodal).** Node V connected to 12 V through 2 Ω, to ground through 4 Ω and 4 Ω: (V − 12)/2 + V/4 + V/4 = 0 ⇒ V(1/2 + 1/2) = 6 ⇒ V = 6 V.

steps.title: Which method?
steps.body: Fewer meshes than nodes? Use mesh. Many parallel branches and current sources? Use nodal. Both give the same answer — pick the one with fewer equations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that a shared resistor's voltage uses (I₁ − I₂).
- Wrong reference node signs.
- Not converting a current source into a supermesh constraint.

quiz.why: With n nodes, one is chosen as the reference, leaving n − 1 independent nodal equations.
Mesh analysis applies Kirchhoff's voltage law around each independent mesh (loop).
A supernode is formed when a voltage source connects two non-reference nodes, so that the two nodes are treated together.
options: a current source is in a mesh
a voltage source joins two non-reference nodes

quiz.why: If meshes are both taken clockwise, a resistor shared by two meshes has mesh currents in opposite directions, so the current through it is I₁ − I₂.

lessons.title: Superposition, Thevenin and Norton theorems

scenes.text: A designer tests 10 different loads on the same complicated circuit.
Thevenin reduces the circuit to one source and one resistor — each load is then a one-line calculation.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body: In a linear circuit with several sources, the response = sum of responses to each source acting alone (other voltage sources shorted, current sources opened). Not valid for power directly (power is non-linear).

steps.title: Thevenin and Norton
steps.body:
Any linear two-terminal network = V_th in series with R_th (Thevenin) or I_N in parallel with R_N (Norton).
V_th = open-circuit voltage; I_N = short-circuit current; R_th = R_N = resistance seen with independent sources deactivated = V_th/I_N.
Load current I_L = V_th/(R_th + R_L).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Thevenin).** 24 V source with 4 Ω series, then 12 Ω across terminals A–B. V_th = 24 × 12/16 = 18 V; R_th = 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω. For R_L = 6 Ω: I_L = 18/9 = 2 A.

**Example 2 (Norton).** Same: I_N = 24/4 = 6 A (12 Ω shorted); R_N = 3 Ω; check V_th = 6 × 3 = 18 V ✔

**Example 3 (superposition).** 10 V source with 5 Ω, a 2 A current source, common 5 Ω load: from V alone I = 1 A; from I alone (V shorted) I = 1 A in load ⇒ total 2 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Opening voltage sources (they must be shorted) when finding R_th.
- Including the load resistor when finding V_th.
- Superposing powers.

items: Remove the load from terminals A–B
Deactivate independent sources (V short, I open)

quiz.why: To find R_th, independent voltage sources are short-circuited, because an ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance.
The Norton current is the current through a short circuit placed across the output terminals.
R_th = V_th/I_N, the open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current.

quiz.q: Superposition cannot be used to find
quiz.why: Superposition holds for linear quantities (current and voltage), but power is proportional to the square, so it cannot be added directly.
Thevenin's theorem applies to linear networks, where superposition and Ohm's law hold.

lessons.title: Maximum power transfer and source transformation

story.title: Getting the most from a solar panel

scenes.text: A small solar charger delivers the most power only into the right load.
Maximum power transfer: match the load to the source's internal resistance.

steps.title: Maximum power transfer
steps.body: Power to R_L is maximum when R_L = R_th: P_max = V_th²/(4R_th). Efficiency at that point is only 50% — used in communication/signal circuits, not in power distribution.

steps.title: Source transformation
steps.body: A voltage source V with series R ⇔ current source V/R with parallel R. Useful for combining sources and simplifying before mesh/nodal analysis.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_th = 18 V, R_th = 3 Ω ⇒ R_L = 3 Ω, P_max = 324/12 = 27 W.

**Example 2.** At R_L = 6 Ω: I = 2 A, P = 24 W (less than 27 W).

**Example 3.** 12 V with 4 Ω ⇔ 3 A source with 4 Ω in parallel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking maximum power means maximum efficiency.
- Using P_max = V²/R_th (missing the factor 4).
- Forgetting to keep the same resistor in source transformation.

activity.label: Load resistance for a source with V_th = 12 V, R_th = 4 Ω

bands.text: Below R_th: high current, less than maximum power, poor efficiency.
Near R_L = R_th: maximum power (9 W) at 50% efficiency.
Above R_th: less power but higher efficiency.

quiz.why: Maximum power is transferred to a load when R_L = R_th.
At R_L = R_th, the current is V_th/(2R_th), so P_max = (V_th/2R_th)² R_th = V_th²/(4R_th).
At matching, the same power is lost in R_th as is delivered to the load, so the efficiency is 50%.
Source transformation: a voltage source V with series R is equivalent to a current source V/R = 10/2 = 5 A in parallel with R = 2 Ω.

quiz.q: Power grids avoid matched loads because
quiz.why: Power systems avoid matched loads because half the power would be wasted in the source and lines (efficiency only 50%).

Solve series and parallel RLC circuits with phasors
Calculate active, reactive and apparent power and power factor
